Procedures and surgery: removing the fibroids while keeping the womb (myomectomy), blocking their blood supply (uterine artery embolisation), or removing the womb (hysterectomy). Some private hospitals in Malaysia also offer focused ultrasound (HIFU) for selected patients. Fibroids don’t turn into cancer. A rare cancer of the womb muscle, leiomyosarcoma, affects fewer than 1 in 1,000 women thought to have fibroids. What is a Bartholin cyst? A fluid-filled swelling of one of the Bartholin glands, which sit either side of the vaginal opening. It is usually painless unless it becomes infected. Will a Bartholin cyst go away on its own? Small cysts often do, and warm baths can help them drain. A painful or infected cyst (abscess) needs a doctor. Is a Bartholin cyst an STI? Usually not. Most infections are caused by common bacteria, although an STI is occasionally involved, so testing may be offered. Are ovarian cysts dangerous? Most are harmless and disappear within a few months. Sudden severe pain with vomiting or fainting needs emergency care, as a cyst may have twisted or burst. Do ovarian cysts need surgery? Only some do, such as large, persistent or unusual cysts. Most are simply rechecked with an ultrasound. What are the symptoms of fibroids? Heavy or painful periods, pressure in the tummy, needing to pass urine often and pain during sex. Many women have no symptoms. Can fibroids turn into cancer? No. Fibroids aren’t cancer and don’t turn into it. A rare cancer of the womb muscle can look similar, but it is very uncommon. What are the warning signs of ovarian cancer? Persistent bloating, pelvic or tummy pain, feeling full quickly and needing to pass urine more often, on most days. See a doctor if these are new.

title: Trigger finger, carpal tunnel and other hand pain: symptoms, treatment and when to see a doctor
desc: A finger that clicks or locks, or a hand that goes numb at night, are common problems, especially in women over 40 and people with diabetes. What trigger finger, carpal tunnel syndrome and De Quervain’s are, what helps, when surgery is worth it, and when numbness is an emergency.
headings: Trigger finger · Carpal tunnel syndrome (kebas tangan) · De Quervain’s tenosynovitis (thumb and wrist pain) · Other causes of hand numbness · Check your blood sugar · When to see a doctor
keywords: Guides Trigger finger and carpal tunnel Trigger finger Carpal tunnel syndrome De Quervain’s tenosynovitis kencing manis gula hba1c mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Trigger finger causes a finger or thumb to catch, click or lock when bent, often worse in the morning, with a tender lump at the base of the finger. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes numbness, tingling and pain in the thumb, index, middle and ring fingers, often waking you at night. Both are more common in women aged 40 to 60, in pregnancy and in people with diabetes. Diabetes about doubles the risk of trigger finger. Splints, rest and steroid injections help many people. A short operation under local anaesthetic usually cures both conditions if other treatment fails. Sudden numbness or weakness in one arm, with a drooping face or slurred speech, could be a stroke. Call 999. Each finger is bent by a tendon that slides through a tunnel of tough bands at the base of the finger. In trigger finger , the tendon or a small lump on it catches on the first band, so the finger gets stuck when you bend it, then clicks or pops straight. Symptoms: clicking, catching or locking of a finger or thumb a finger stuck bent that you have to straighten with your other hand pain and a tender lump on the palm, at the base of the finger symptoms that are often worse first thing in the morning Who gets it: it is more common in women aged 40 to 60, and in people with diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis. In a large Swedish study, diabetes doubled the risk. Babies and young children can have a different form, “trigger thumb”, which should be seen by a doctor. Treatment: Rest and splinting: avoiding activities that cause pain, and a splint that keeps the finger straight, often at night. Steroid injection into the tendon sheath works for about 7 in 10 people, though it can take days to weeks. A second injection sometimes helps. It works less well in people with diabetes, and can raise blood sugar for 10 to 14 days in those on insulin, so check your levels. Surgery (trigger finger release): a short day-case operation under local anaesthetic to widen the tight band. You can use the hand lightly the same day. The wound heals in a few weeks, though stiffness can take a few months to settle. The problem rarely comes back. A needle release is an alternative some surgeons offer. The median nerve passes through a narrow tunnel in the wrist. In carpal tunnel syndrome , it gets squeezed. Symptoms: numbness, tingling or pins and needles in the thumb, index, middle and ring fingers , but not usually the little finger pain or aching in the hand or wrist symptoms that are worse at night and may wake you, often eased by shaking the hand a weak grip, clumsiness or dropping things, and in severe cases wasting of the muscle at the base of the thumb Risk factors: pregnancy, being overweight, diabetes, an underactive thyroid, rheumatoid arthritis, repetitive gripping or wrist bending, and using vibrating tools. In a Malaysian hospital study of patients having surgery, 8 in 10 were women, the average age was 53, and nearly a third had diabetes. See our guide to thyroid problems . Diagnosis is usually made by examination. A nerve conduction test may be done if the diagnosis is unclear or surgery is being considered. Treatment: Wrist splint at night to keep the wrist straight. It can take up to 6 weeks to help. Steroid injection can relieve symptoms, though often for a limited time. Surgery (carpal tunnel release): about 20 minutes under local anaesthetic, usually without an overnight stay. Night symptoms often ease within a week, most people return to normal activities in about a month, and grip strength returns over 2 to 3 months. Surgery is recommended sooner for constant numbness or muscle wasting, to prevent permanent nerve damage. In pregnancy , it often settles within months of the birth. Diabetes makes trigger finger and carpal tunnel syndrome more likely, so a blood sugar check is worthwhile. De Quervain’s causes pain on the thumb side of the wrist , worse when gripping, lifting or twisting, from inflamed tendons. It is common in women in their 40s and 50s, and in new mothers , often starting a month or two after the birth, partly from lifting the baby. A doctor may test it by asking you to tuck your thumb into your fist and bend your wrist towards the little finger, which causes pain. Treatment includes a thumb splint, ice, anti-inflammatory painkillers and a steroid injection. Surgery is an option if it doesn’t improve. A trapped nerve in the neck , causing neck pain running down the arm with tingling or weakness. See our guide to slipped discs . The ulnar nerve at the elbow , causing numbness in the ring and little fingers, worse with the elbow bent. See a doctor if it lasts more than 6 weeks, as muscle weakness can become permanent. Diabetes , which can damage nerves in the hands and feet. Low vitamin B12 . See our guide to anaemia . Call 999 straight away for sudden numbness or weakness in an arm or leg, especially on one side, with a drooping face, slurred speech, loss of balance or vision changes, even if it passes. These are signs of a stroke. See our guide to stroke and heart attack . Hand problems such as trigger finger, carpal tunnel syndrome and frozen shoulder are all more common with diabetes. In Malaysia, 15.6% of adults have diabetes, and 2 in 5 of them don’t know it. If you develop any of these, ask for a blood sugar test. See our guide to normal blood sugar levels . a finger that keeps locking, or that you can’t straighten numbness or tingling that keeps coming back, wakes you at night, or doesn’t improve with a splint weakness, clumsiness or muscle wasting in your hand a hot, swollen, red finger or hand, which could be an infection What causes trigger finger? A tendon or a small lump on it catches on a tight band at the base of the finger. It is more common in women aged 40 to 60 and in people with diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis. Can trigger finger go away on its own? Sometimes, especially with rest and a splint. Many people need a steroid injection, and some need a short operation. How effective is a steroid injection for trigger finger? It works for about 7 in 10 people, but less well in people with diabetes. A second injection is sometimes given. What are the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome? Numbness, tingling and pain in the thumb, index, middle and ring fingers, often worse at night, sometimes with a weak grip. Why do my hands go numb at night? Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common cause, as the wrist often bends during sleep. A night splint can help. How long does it take to recover from carpal tunnel surgery? Most people return to normal activities in about a month, and grip strength returns over 2 to 3 months. What is De Quervain’s? Painful, inflamed tendons on the thumb side of the wrist, common in new mothers and in women in their 40s and 50s. When is hand numbness an emergency? When it is sudden and comes with weakness, a drooping face, slurred speech or loss of balance, which may be a stroke. Call 999.

title: Gestational diabetes and the BSP chart: the glucose test, normal blood sugar in pregnancy, and what to do
desc: More than 1 in 4 Malaysian mothers in a 2022 survey reported being told they had diabetes in pregnancy. Who needs the glucose tolerance test, what the results mean, the BSP blood sugar targets, how it is managed with diet, metformin or insulin, and why a check after birth matters.
headings: What is gestational diabetes? · Who should be tested? · The glucose test (OGTT / MGTT) · The BSP (blood sugar profile) and targets · Managing gestational diabetes · Why control matters · After the birth
keywords: Women's health Gestational diabetes and BSP Gestational diabetes Oral glucose tolerance test Diabetes in pregnancy kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal klinik doctor doktor gp
body: In the National Health and Morbidity Survey, the share of Malaysian mothers who said they had been told they had diabetes in pregnancy rose from 12.5% in 2016 to 27.1% in 2022. Under Ministry of Health guidelines, women with risk factors have a 75 g glucose test (OGTT/MGTT) at booking and again at 24 to 28 weeks. Women aged 25 or over without other risk factors are tested at 24 to 28 weeks. GDM is diagnosed in Malaysia if fasting glucose is 5.1 mmol/L or more, or the 2-hour result is 7.8 mmol/L or more. BSP (blood sugar profile) targets: before meals 5.3 or lower, 1 hour after meals 7.8 or lower, 2 hours after meals 6.7 or lower. About half of women with GDM later develop type 2 diabetes, so have a glucose test about 6 weeks after the birth, then yearly checks. During pregnancy, hormones from the placenta make the body less responsive to insulin. Most women make enough extra insulin to cope. In gestational diabetes, the body can’t keep up, and blood sugar rises. It usually develops in the second half of pregnancy and goes away after delivery. It usually causes no symptoms , which is why testing matters. A few women notice more thirst, passing more urine or tiredness, which are also common in normal pregnancy. In Malaysia, it is becoming much more common. The share of mothers in the National Health and Morbidity Survey who said they had been told they had diabetes in pregnancy more than doubled between 2016 and 2022, to 27.1%. The risk was higher with older age, overweight, obesity and high blood pressure. The Ministry of Health’s guideline on diabetes in pregnancy lists these risk factors: BMI over 27 (see our BMI calculator ) gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy a parent, brother or sister with diabetes a previous baby weighing more than 4 kg a previous unexplained stillbirth, baby with birth defects, or difficult birth with the baby’s shoulder stuck sugar in the urine on two occasions high blood pressure, too much fluid around the baby, or taking steroid medicines Timing: With a risk factor: a glucose tolerance test at your first antenatal visit (booking), repeated at 24 to 28 weeks if normal. Aged 25 or over with no other risk factor: a test at 24 to 28 weeks. The guideline notes that testing every pregnant woman is ideal where resources allow. HbA1c and random blood sugar tests aren’t used to diagnose gestational diabetes. See our guide to early pregnancy and booking . In Malaysian clinics, the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test is often called the MGTT or MOGTT (modified glucose tolerance test). Fast overnight for at least 8 hours. Plain water is usually allowed. A blood sample is taken (fasting glucose). You drink a sweet drink containing 75 g of glucose, within a few minutes. Rest quietly for 2 hours. Don’t eat, and avoid walking around. A second blood sample is taken at 2 hours. Result (mmol/L) Normal Gestational diabetes Fasting Below 5.1 5.1 or more 2 hours after the drink Below 7.8 7.8 or more Either result being high is enough for a diagnosis. Much higher results, such as fasting 7.0 or more, may mean diabetes that was already there before pregnancy, and need a repeat test. Malaysia uses a lower 2-hour cut-off than some international criteria. For normal blood sugar outside pregnancy, see our guide to blood sugar levels . After diagnosis, your blood sugar is checked several times a day to see how well it is controlled. A BSP (blood sugar profile) is a set of these checks, traditionally done at the clinic or in hospital. The guideline prefers home monitoring with a fingerprick meter, as it better reflects everyday levels. Where that isn’t possible, a clinic BSP is done about every 2 weeks until delivery. When Target (mmol/L) Fasting and before meals 5.3 or lower 1 hour after starting a meal 7.8 or lower 2 hours after starting a meal 6.7 or lower Your clinic will tell you whether to test 1 or 2 hours after meals, and how often. If you are on diet alone or one type of medicine, it is usually at least once a day until you reach your targets. If you take insulin or metformin, keep your readings above 4.0, and learn the signs of low blood sugar: shaking, sweating, hunger or confusion. Write down every reading, with the time and what you ate, and bring the record, along with your pink book , to every check-up. Diet is the first step. The Malaysian guideline recommends a carbohydrate-controlled meal plan, with at least 175 g of carbohydrate a day spread across meals, and low-GI choices: Keep rice, noodles and bread to measured portions. The guideline’s sample menu uses 2 ladles of rice at lunch and dinner. Choose wholegrains and plenty of vegetables, and include protein with each meal. Sugar counts towards your carbohydrates. Choose plain water instead of sweetened drinks. Have smaller, regular meals and snacks rather than large ones. A dietitian can tailor a plan to the foods you eat. Smaller portions of rice and noodles, with more vegetables and protein, help keep blood sugar in range. Activity: 20 to 30 minutes of moderate exercise on most days, such as brisk walking, swimming or pregnancy yoga, unless your doctor advises otherwise. Medicines: if targets aren’t reached within 1 to 2 weeks of diet and exercise, a doctor may start metformin tablets, and insulin if needed. Insulin is started straight away if fasting sugar is very high. Both are safe in pregnancy, and insulin can usually be started without a hospital stay. Delivery: women controlled by diet alone without complications are usually advised to deliver by 40 weeks, and those on medicines between 37 and 39 weeks. Your obstetrician will plan this with you. Uncontrolled gestational diabetes can lead to: a large baby , making birth more difficult, including the baby’s shoulder getting stuck more need for induction or caesarean birth pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure in pregnancy) premature birth and too much fluid around the baby low blood sugar and jaundice in the baby after birth rarely, stillbirth Treatment works: the Malaysian guideline notes that treating gestational diabetes lowers the risk of pre-eclampsia, shoulder problems at birth and large babies. Most women can stop insulin or tablets as soon as the baby is born. Have a glucose tolerance test about 6 weeks after delivery , then a check every year. About half of women with gestational diabetes go on to develop type 2 diabetes. Breastfeeding for at least 3 months is linked to a lower risk of later diabetes. Keep active and aim for a healthy weight. In a future pregnancy, you will have a glucose test early, at booking. Tell your doctor before trying to conceive. What is a normal BSP in pregnancy? Malaysian targets are 5.3 mmol/L or lower before meals, 7.8 or lower 1 hour after a meal, and 6.7 or lower 2 hours after a meal. What does BSP mean? Blood sugar profile: a series of blood sugar checks through the day, before and after meals, to monitor diabetes in pregnancy. What is the MGTT test? The 75 g oral glucose tolerance test: a fasting blood test, a sugary drink, then another blood test 2 hours later. What result means gestational diabetes? In Malaysia, a fasting glucose of 5.1 mmol/L or more, or a 2-hour result of 7.8 mmol/L or more. When is the glucose test done in pregnancy? At booking if you have risk factors, and at 24 to 28 weeks. Women aged 25 or over without other risk factors are tested at 24 to 28 weeks. Will gestational diabetes harm my baby? Well-controlled gestational diabetes usually leads to a healthy baby. Poor control raises the risk of a large baby, birth complications and low blood sugar after birth. Does gestational diabetes go away after birth? Usually, yes, but about half of women later develop type 2 diabetes, so have a glucose test about 6 weeks after delivery and yearly checks. Can I eat rice with gestational diabetes? Yes, in measured portions as part of a carbohydrate-controlled plan, with plenty of vegetables and protein. A dietitian can help.

title: Rotavirus in babies and children: symptoms, dehydration warning signs, and the rotavirus vaccine
desc: Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhoea in young children, and is estimated to put about 31,000 Malaysian children in hospital each year. The symptoms, how to keep your child hydrated, the danger signs, and the oral vaccine, which parents in Malaysia currently get privately.
headings: What is rotavirus? · Symptoms · Caring for your child at home · Dehydration warning signs · The rotavirus vaccine · The rotavirus vaccine in Malaysia · Stopping it spreading
keywords: Prevention Rotavirus and the vaccine Rotavirus Rotavirus vaccine Gastroenteritis payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhoea in children under 5. It is most severe between about 6 months and 2 years. Symptoms are vomiting, frequent watery diarrhoea, fever and tummy pain, usually lasting 3 to 8 days. The main danger is dehydration. Keep breastfeeding or formula feeding, and give oral rehydration solution in small, frequent sips. The vaccine is given as drops by mouth in 2 or 3 doses, starting at about 2 months. The first dose must be given before 15 weeks and all doses before 8 months. It isn’t in Malaysia’s National Immunisation Programme. Ask your clinic early, as the age limits are strict. Rotavirus infects the gut and causes gastroenteritis (a stomach bug). The World Health Organization calls it the leading cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhoea in children under 5 worldwide. It spreads very easily , through tiny amounts of stool on hands, toys, surfaces and food. Children can pass it on before they have symptoms and for days after they recover, and the virus survives well on surfaces. Who gets it: almost all children catch it at least once by age 5. The most severe illness is in unvaccinated children aged about 3 months to 3 years, and Malaysian health officials have said those aged 6 months to 2 years are most vulnerable. In Malaysia, a 2016 study estimated that rotavirus causes about 31,000 hospital admissions, 41,000 outpatient visits and 27 deaths each year in children under 5. In hospitals in Kuala Lumpur and Kuala Terengganu, 38% of tested stool samples from young children admitted with gastroenteritis were positive for rotavirus, and the costs were a heavy burden for many families. Symptoms usually start about 2 days after exposure: sudden vomiting , often first frequent, watery diarrhoea fever tummy pain and loss of appetite Vomiting and diarrhoea usually last 3 to 8 days . Other viruses and bacteria cause similar illness. See our guide to food poisoning and gastroenteritis . Keep breastfeeding , or keep giving formula made up at its usual strength, in smaller, more frequent feeds. Give oral rehydration solution (ORS) from a pharmacy, mixed exactly as the pack says, in small sips every few minutes, especially after each vomit or loose stool. A spoon or syringe can help. Avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse. Offer food once your child wants to eat. Don’t give anti-diarrhoea medicine to children. Paracetamol can help with fever and discomfort. See our guide to fever in children . See a doctor urgently if your child: has fewer wet nappies or passes little urine has a dry mouth, cries with few or no tears, or has sunken eyes in babies, has a sunken soft spot (fontanelle) on the head is drowsy, irritable, or drinking poorly can’t keep fluids down, or has been vomiting for more than 2 days has blood in the stool, or green vomit is a young baby, especially under 6 months Go to an emergency department if your child is very drowsy or hard to wake, is breathing fast, or has pale, blotchy, blue or cold skin. These are signs of severe dehydration. See our guide on clinic or emergency department . Keep feeding and give small, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution to prevent dehydration. The rotavirus vaccine is given as drops into the mouth , not an injection. There are two types: a 2-dose vaccine, usually at about 2 and 4 months a 3-dose vaccine, usually at about 2, 4 and 6 months Timing is strict: the first dose should be given before 15 weeks of age, and all doses by 8 months. If your baby misses these windows, they can’t start the course later, so plan ahead with your clinic. How well it works: the vaccine prevents about 9 in 10 cases of severe rotavirus illness in countries like the US, with somewhat lower protection in some lower-income settings. It doesn’t prevent every bout of diarrhoea, but makes severe illness and hospital stays much less likely. Safety: it is very safe. Mild fussiness or loose stools can follow. There is a very small risk of intussusception , where part of the bowel folds into itself, estimated at about 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 100,000 babies, mostly in the week after a dose. The World Health Organization says the benefits far outweigh this risk. See a doctor urgently if, after a dose, your baby has bouts of severe crying, pulls their legs up to the chest, vomits repeatedly or has blood in the stool. The vaccine virus is passed in the stool for a few weeks afterwards, so wash your hands well after nappy changes. The rotavirus vaccine is not part of Malaysia’s National Immunisation Programme , so it isn’t given free at Klinik Kesihatan. Parents usually get it at private clinics and hospitals. Malaysian paediatricians have long called for it to be added to the national programme, and a university workshop in August 2026 highlighted the gap. Ask your clinic about it at your baby’s 2-month check, alongside the routine vaccines. See our baby vaccination schedule . Wash hands well with soap and water after nappy changes and toilet use, and before preparing food. Clean toys, changing areas and toilet surfaces often. Keep children home from nursery or school until 2 days after the diarrhoea and vomiting have stopped. Don’t share towels, cups or utensils during the illness. Handwashing helps, but because rotavirus spreads so easily, vaccination is the best protection. What are the symptoms of rotavirus? Sudden vomiting, frequent watery diarrhoea, fever and tummy pain, usually lasting 3 to 8 days. How long is rotavirus contagious? From before symptoms start until a few days after recovery. Keep children home until 2 days after the diarrhoea and vomiting stop. How do I treat rotavirus at home? Keep breastfeeding or formula feeding, give oral rehydration solution in small, frequent sips, and watch for dehydration. Don’t give anti-diarrhoea medicine to children. When should I take my child to hospital? If they are very drowsy, have far fewer wet nappies, can’t keep fluids down, have sunken eyes or a sunken soft spot, blood in the stool, or cold, pale or blotchy skin. Is the rotavirus vaccine free in Malaysia? No. It isn’t part of the National Immunisation Programme, so it is available at private clinics and hospitals. When should my baby get the rotavirus vaccine? Usually at 2 and 4 months, or 2, 4 and 6 months depending on the vaccine. The first dose must be before 15 weeks and all doses by 8 months. Is the rotavirus vaccine safe? Yes. There is a very small risk of intussusception, a bowel problem, mostly in the week after a dose. Experts agree the benefits far outweigh this. Can my child get rotavirus more than once? Yes, but later infections are usually milder, and vaccination makes severe illness much less likely.

title: URTI and the common cold (selsema): symptoms, what helps, antibiotics, and when to see a doctor
desc: URTI is one of the most common reasons Malaysians see a GP. Almost all are viral colds that clear in 1 to 2 weeks. What URTI means, the remedies that actually help, why antibiotics don’t, how to treat children safely, and the signs that need a doctor.
headings: What is URTI? · Symptoms and how long they last · What helps (ubat selsema) · Colds in children · Why antibiotics don’t help · When to see a doctor · Stopping it spreading
keywords: Guides URTI and the common cold Upper respiratory tract infection Common cold Selsema denggi aedes nyamuk mosquito kencing manis gula hba1c vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp
body: URTI covers colds, sore throats, sinusitis and laryngitis. More than 200 viruses cause colds, most often rhinovirus. Cold symptoms build over 2 to 3 days and usually clear within 1 to 2 weeks. A cough can last 3 to 4 weeks. Rest, fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen, saline nose drops and honey for coughs (not under 1 year) help. Zinc and vitamin C have only small or uncertain effects. Antibiotics don’t help colds and cause side effects in about 1 in 10 people. In a national study of Malaysian clinics, 46% of URTI patients were still given them. See a doctor for breathing difficulty, fever lasting more than 3 days, symptoms that get better then worse, or a baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more. Doctors write URTI on MCs and notes to mean an infection of the upper airways: the nose, sinuses, throat and voice box. It includes: the common cold ( selsema ) sore throat and tonsillitis sinusitis laryngitis (a hoarse or lost voice) More than 200 viruses cause colds, most often rhinovirus , as well as common coronaviruses, adenovirus and others. In a 2014 national survey of Malaysian primary care clinics, URTI was the most common diagnosis among patients given antibiotics, accounting for about half of all antibiotic prescriptions. a blocked or runny nose ( hidung tersumbat ), sneezing sore or scratchy throat cough mild fever, aches and tiredness, especially in children hoarse voice, and pressure in the ears or face Symptoms build over 2 to 3 days, and most colds clear within 1 to 2 weeks . A cough can carry on for 3 to 4 weeks . Green or yellow mucus is normal in a cold and doesn’t mean you need antibiotics. Cold, flu, COVID-19 or dengue? A cold starts gradually and mainly affects the nose and throat. You can usually carry on. Flu comes on within hours, with high fever, aches and exhaustion. COVID-19 can look very similar to a cold or flu. A test is the only way to tell. Dengue usually causes a high fever, headache, pain behind the eyes and body aches, often without a runny nose. If you have a high fever without cold symptoms, see a doctor. Rest and drink plenty of fluids. Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever, sore throat and aches. If dengue is possible, use paracetamol only. See our guide to painkillers . Saline (salt-water) nose drops or spray may ease a blocked nose, and are safe for children. Honey , alone or in warm water with lemon, can ease a cough. A Cochrane review found it probably helps children’s cough for up to 3 days. Never give honey to babies under 1. Gargling with warm salt water can soothe a sore throat in adults. Decongestant nasal sprays can give a small improvement in a blocked nose, but don’t use them for more than a week, and not in children under 6. Supplements: Vitamin C taken regularly doesn’t stop you catching colds, and may only slightly shorten them. Starting it once you are ill shows no consistent benefit. Zinc may shorten a cold by about 2 days, but the evidence is weak, and it can cause nausea and taste changes. Steam inhalation hasn’t been shown to help, and bowls of hot water can scald children. Combination cold remedies: many contain paracetamol, so don’t take them with separate paracetamol, to avoid an overdose. Antihistamines help a little only in the first 1 to 2 days. Most colds clear within 1 to 2 weeks with rest, fluids and simple remedies. Young children often have 6 or more colds a year, especially in nursery or school. Malaysia’s Drug Control Authority says cough and cold medicines containing antihistamines, decongestants or cough suppressants shouldn’t be given to children under 2 , and only on a doctor’s or pharmacist’s advice for those aged 2 to 6. Use saline drops, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen, dosed by weight. Don’t give aspirin to children under 16. Honey is fine from age 1. Avoid throat lozenges under 4, as they are a choking risk. See our guides to fever in children and RSV , which can make babies very unwell. Colds and most URTIs are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only work on bacteria. A 2025 Cochrane review found antibiotics don’t help colds , even with green or yellow mucus, and adults who took them had about 2.6 times the risk of side effects such as diarrhoea, nausea and rash. In a 2014 national survey of Malaysian clinics, 46% of URTI patients were prescribed antibiotics, 58% at private clinics and 17% at public clinics. Unnecessary antibiotics fuel antibiotic resistance , making future infections harder to treat. Malaysia has a national action plan to reduce this. If your doctor isn’t sure, they may suggest a “just in case” prescription to collect only if you aren’t improving after a few days. Studies show this greatly reduces antibiotic use, with similar recovery. Antibiotics may be needed for some bacterial throat infections, sinus infections that last more than about 10 days, or complications such as pneumonia . Your doctor will decide. See a doctor if: you have a fever lasting more than 3 days you are breathless, wheezy, or have chest pain you get better, then worse again symptoms haven’t improved after 10 days, or a cough lasts more than 3 weeks (see our guide to a cough that won’t go away ) you have ear pain, or severe pain in the face or forehead you have a long-term condition such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease, or a weak immune system you are showing signs of dehydration Get urgent help for difficulty breathing, coughing up blood, a swollen, painful neck on one side, or a baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more (3 to 6 months: 39°C or more). See our guide on clinic or emergency department . You are infectious from a few days before symptoms until they have gone. Wash your hands often, use and bin tissues, and cough into your elbow. Don’t share towels or cups, and stay home if you have a fever. The yearly flu vaccine doesn’t prevent colds, but does protect against flu. If you need time off work, see our guide to medical certificates . An MC requires an in-person examination. What does URTI mean? Upper respiratory tract infection: an infection of the nose, sinuses, throat or voice box, most often a common cold. It is usually caused by a virus. How long does a cold last? Most colds clear within 1 to 2 weeks. A cough can last 3 to 4 weeks. Do I need antibiotics for URTI? Usually not. Most URTIs are viral, and antibiotics don’t help them but can cause side effects and resistance. What is the best medicine for a cold (ubat selsema)? Rest, fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen, saline nose drops and honey for a cough. Decongestant sprays can help for a few days. Does vitamin C cure a cold? No. Taking it regularly doesn’t prevent colds and may only slightly shorten them. Starting it once ill shows no consistent benefit. Can I give cough and cold medicine to my child? Not under 2, and only on a doctor’s or pharmacist’s advice for ages 2 to 6. Saline drops, fluids and paracetamol are safer choices. Is green mucus a sign of infection needing antibiotics? No. Green or yellow mucus is common in viral colds and doesn’t mean you need antibiotics. When should I see a doctor for a cold? For fever over 3 days, breathlessness or chest pain, getting worse after improving, or symptoms lasting more than 10 days.

title: Normal heart rate and palpitations (jantung berdebar): what’s normal, how to check your pulse, and when it’s a problem
desc: A normal resting heart rate for adults is 60 to 100 beats a minute. What changes it, how to take your pulse properly, what palpitations and skipped beats usually mean, why an irregular pulse after 65 should be checked for atrial fibrillation, and the warning signs that need emergency help.
headings: What is a normal heart rate? (Kadar degupan jantung normal) · How to check your pulse · Fast and slow heart rates · Palpitations (jantung berdebar) · Atrial fibrillation · Tests a doctor may do · When to get help
keywords: Heart & diabetes Heart rate and palpitations Heart rate Palpitations Atrial fibrillation kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp
body: A normal resting heart rate for adults is 60 to 100 beats a minute. Very fit people may be in the 40s or 50s. Check your pulse at rest: count the beats for 30 seconds and double it, or for a full minute if it feels irregular. Palpitations are usually caused by caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stress, poor sleep or exercise, and skipped beats are usually harmless. An irregular pulse, especially from age 65, can be atrial fibrillation, which makes a stroke about 5 times more likely but can be treated. Call 999 for palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness, fainting or dizziness, or a heartbeat that won’t settle. Adults: a normal resting heart rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute (bpm) . Women tend to be slightly higher than men. Regular exercise lowers your resting rate, and athletes often have rates in the 40s or 50s. Children have faster heart rates. Typical ranges from the Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne are: Age Heart rate (bpm) Newborn 120–170 1 year 105–150 2 to 4 years 80–150 6 to 8 years 70–140 10 to 12 years 60–130 14 years and over 60–115 These ranges are wide, and a child’s heart rate rises with fever, crying and activity. What changes your heart rate: exercise, fever or infection, heat, dehydration, caffeine, alcohol, smoking, stress or anxiety, poor sleep, pregnancy, anaemia, an overactive thyroid and some medicines, including asthma inhalers (which raise it) and beta-blockers (which lower it). Sit quietly for 5 minutes first. Avoid caffeine and smoking beforehand. Place two fingers (not your thumb) on the inside of your wrist, at the base of your thumb, or on your neck beside your windpipe. Count the beats for 30 seconds and double it . If the beat feels irregular, count for a full 60 seconds . Notice whether the rhythm is regular, like a ticking clock, or irregular. Smartwatches can measure your heart rate and some can alert you to an irregular rhythm. In a large study, only about a third of people who got an irregular-rhythm alert were found to have atrial fibrillation on a follow-up heart monitor. An alert is a reason to see a doctor, not a diagnosis, and no alert doesn’t rule out a problem. A home blood pressure monitor also shows your pulse. See our guide to checking your blood pressure at home . Fast (tachycardia): over 100 bpm at rest. Most often it is a normal response to exercise, fever, anxiety, caffeine, alcohol, dehydration, low blood sugar, anaemia or pregnancy. Sometimes it is a heart rhythm problem such as: SVT (supraventricular tachycardia): sudden episodes of a very fast, regular heartbeat that start and stop abruptly, lasting minutes to hours. It is usually not serious. A doctor may teach you a breathing-and-straining technique (a modified Valsalva manoeuvre) to stop episodes, which worked in about 4 in 10 people in a UK trial. Atrial fibrillation: see below. Slow (bradycardia): under 60 bpm. It is often normal in fit people and during sleep. A rate of 40 to 60 without symptoms is usually not a worry. It can also be caused by medicines such as beta-blockers, an underactive thyroid , sleep apnoea, ageing or heart conduction problems. A slow rate with dizziness, fainting, breathlessness or tiredness needs checking. A rate below 40 that isn’t normal for you, with symptoms, needs emergency care. Palpitations are when you become aware of your heartbeat: pounding, racing, fluttering or skipping. They are very common and usually harmless . Common triggers: caffeine (coffee, tea, energy drinks), alcohol and nicotine, including vapes stress, anxiety and panic. See our guide to anxiety . exercise, and lack of sleep pregnancy and the menopause fever, dehydration and low blood sugar medicines and products such as decongestants in cold remedies, asthma inhalers, thyroid medicines and some supplements anaemia and an overactive thyroid Skipped or extra beats (ectopic beats) feel like a missed beat followed by a thump. According to the British Heart Foundation, they are usually harmless and don’t damage the heart. They are more noticeable with stress, poor sleep, alcohol and caffeine. Regular exercise lowers your resting heart rate over time. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common heart rhythm problem. The heart beats irregularly and often fast. Some people feel palpitations, breathlessness or tiredness, but many have no symptoms. It becomes more common from age 55, and is more common in men, and in people with high blood pressure or heart disease. AF makes a stroke about 5 times more likely , because blood clots can form in the heart. See our guide to stroke and heart attack . A Malaysian study found AF in about 0.5% of adults aged 30 and over. Treatment includes medicines to control the heart rate or rhythm, and blood-thinning medicines , which greatly lower stroke risk. Asia Pacific heart rhythm experts recommend checking the pulse or an ECG opportunistically from age 65, for example at a routine clinic visit. an ECG (heart tracing) a 24 to 48 hour heart monitor (Holter), or a longer patch monitor if symptoms come and go an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) blood tests for anaemia, thyroid problems and salts such as potassium. See our guide to blood test results . Try to note when palpitations happen, how long they last, and whether they feel regular or irregular. If you can, record your pulse or an ECG on a smartwatch during an episode. Call 999 or go to an emergency department if palpitations: come with chest pain , breathlessness, dizziness, or you faint or nearly faint don’t stop start during exercise See a doctor soon if: palpitations keep coming back, or last more than a few minutes your pulse is often irregular, especially if you are 65 or over your resting heart rate is regularly above 100 or below 50 with symptoms you have a heart condition, or a family history of heart problems or sudden death at a young age What is a normal heart rate? 60 to 100 beats per minute at rest for adults. Very fit people may be lower, in the 40s or 50s. What is a normal heart rate for children? It is faster than in adults and falls with age, from about 120 to 170 in newborns to about 60 to 115 in teenagers. How do I check my pulse? Rest for 5 minutes, place two fingers on your wrist or neck, and count the beats for 30 seconds and double it, or count for 60 seconds if it feels irregular. Are palpitations dangerous? Usually not. Most are caused by caffeine, stress, alcohol or lack of sleep. Get urgent help if they come with chest pain, breathlessness or fainting. What causes skipped heartbeats? Extra (ectopic) beats, which are common and usually harmless, often triggered by stress, poor sleep, caffeine or alcohol. Is a heart rate of 110 at rest normal? It is higher than normal. It is often due to fever, dehydration, anxiety or caffeine, but if it stays high or comes with symptoms, see a doctor. What is atrial fibrillation? An irregular, often fast heart rhythm that raises stroke risk about 5 times. It is treatable with medicines, including blood thinners. Can a smartwatch detect heart problems? It can flag an irregular rhythm, but alerts aren’t a diagnosis. See a doctor for an ECG if you get one.

title: Painkillers explained: paracetamol, ibuprofen, naproxen and mefenamic acid — which to use, safe doses and who should avoid them
desc: Paracetamol and ibuprofen are among the most searched medicines in Malaysia. How they differ, safe adult doses, which works best, who shouldn’t take anti-inflammatory painkillers (including if dengue is possible), the danger of hidden paracetamol, and why unregistered “pain remedies” can contain steroids.
headings: Paracetamol or an anti-inflammatory? · Paracetamol: safe use · NSAIDs: ibuprofen, naproxen and mefenamic acid · Who should avoid NSAIDs · Stronger painkillers · Be careful with “pain remedies” sold online · When to see a doctor
keywords: Guides Painkillers explained Analgesics Paracetamol Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs denggi aedes nyamuk mosquito kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital
body: Paracetamol: adults usually take 500 mg to 1 g at least 4 hours apart, no more than 4 g (eight 500 mg tablets) in 24 hours. Many cold remedies also contain paracetamol, so count it all. Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs work well for inflammation-type pain, such as period pain, dental pain and sprains. Take them with food, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Avoid NSAIDs if dengue is possible, if you have a stomach ulcer, kidney or heart disease, are taking blood thinners, or are 20 or more weeks pregnant. Taking paracetamol and ibuprofen together gave good relief for about 7 in 10 people in studies of short-term pain. A paracetamol overdose needs emergency care even if you feel well. Delaying treatment by more than 24 hours greatly raises the risk of liver damage. Paracetamol NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, mefenamic acid, diclofenac) Good for Headache, fever, general aches, pain in pregnancy Pain with inflammation: period pain, dental pain, sprains and strains, gout, some back pain Stomach Gentle on the stomach Can cause indigestion, ulcers and bleeding. Take with food Main risk Liver damage in overdose Stomach bleeding, kidney problems, raised blood pressure, heart risks at high doses Dengue The safe choice Avoid: increases bleeding risk Pregnancy Usually the preferred painkiller Avoid from 20 weeks, unless a doctor advises How well they work: a 2015 Cochrane overview of non-prescription painkillers, mostly tested on pain after dental surgery, found ibuprofen with paracetamol worked for about 7 in 10 people, and fast-acting ibuprofen also worked well. Paracetamol alone was less effective for this type of pain. Adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen together if needed, as they work differently. Usual adult dose: one or two 500 mg tablets at a time, at least 4 hours apart, and no more than 8 tablets (4 g) in 24 hours . You may need a lower dose if you weigh under 50 kg, have liver or kidney problems, or drink a lot of alcohol. Ask a pharmacist. Check for hidden paracetamol. Many cold and flu remedies contain it. Taking them with paracetamol tablets is a common way to overdose by accident. See a doctor if you still need it after 3 days. Overdose is dangerous even if you feel fine. Paracetamol overdose can cause liver failure, and symptoms may not appear for a day or more. In a study of more than 1,000 overdose cases at two Kuala Lumpur hospitals, treatment started more than 24 hours after the overdose raised the risk of liver damage about 9-fold. If you have taken too much, go to an emergency department straight away . The National Poison Centre (+604 653 6999) can also advise. For children’s doses, see our guide to fever in children . Medicine Usual adult dose Notes Ibuprofen 200 to 400 mg up to 3 times a day, at least 4 hours apart. Up to 1,200 mg a day without a doctor’s advice See a doctor if needed for more than 10 days Naproxen Commonly 250 mg 3 to 4 times a day for short-term pain, sometimes starting with 500 mg Longer-acting Mefenamic acid 500 mg three times a day, started when period pain begins Used mainly for period pain. Stop if you get diarrhoea Diclofenac As prescribed Not for people with heart disease, stroke, poor circulation or heart failure Take them with or after food , at the lowest dose for the shortest time . Don’t take two NSAIDs together , for example ibuprofen with naproxen. At high doses (2,400 mg of ibuprofen a day or more), NSAIDs slightly increase the risk of heart attack and stroke. This risk isn’t seen with ibuprofen at up to 1,200 mg a day. NSAID gels rubbed on painful joints, such as in knee arthritis, help some people and are an option for those who can’t take tablets. See our guides to period pain , gout and back pain . Don’t take ibuprofen, naproxen, mefenamic acid or diclofenac without a doctor’s advice if you: might have dengue . In Malaysia, use paracetamol for any fever until dengue is ruled out. See our dengue guide . have or have had a stomach ulcer or bleeding. See our guide to reflux and ulcers . have kidney disease , heart failure, heart disease, or have had a stroke have high blood pressure that isn’t controlled take blood-thinning medicines, steroids or some antidepressants have asthma that gets worse with aspirin or NSAIDs are 20 or more weeks pregnant . The US Food and Drug Administration warns NSAIDs at this stage can harm the baby’s kidneys. are dehydrated, for example with vomiting or diarrhoea are over 65, without checking with a doctor first A Malaysian national survey found that people who reported kidney disease were more likely to use NSAIDs, suggesting many don’t know they should avoid them. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about your health conditions and other medicines before taking an NSAID. Painkillers containing codeine or tramadol are prescription medicines. They commonly cause constipation and drowsiness, and can cause dependence with regular use, so they are used for short periods. Codeine isn’t usually used while breastfeeding. Don’t drive if they make you drowsy. The Ministry of Health has repeatedly warned about unregistered traditional products, sold for joint or body pain, that were found to contain hidden steroids such as dexamethasone, and NSAIDs such as diclofenac. Taken for long periods, hidden steroids can cause high blood sugar and blood pressure, weak bones and other serious problems. Buy medicines and traditional products only if they have a MAL registration number and security hologram. You can check a product on the NPRA website. Ask a pharmacist before buying painkillers online. pain that hasn’t improved after 3 days of paracetamol or 10 days of ibuprofen you need painkillers most days you have black stools, vomit blood, or severe stomach pain while taking an NSAID you have signs of an allergy, such as swelling or difficulty breathing (call 999) any suspected paracetamol overdose, even if you feel well (go to an emergency department) What is the difference between paracetamol and ibuprofen? Paracetamol eases pain and fever and is gentle on the stomach. Ibuprofen is an anti-inflammatory that works well for inflammation-type pain but can irritate the stomach and isn’t safe in dengue. How much paracetamol can I take in a day? For most adults, no more than 4 g (eight 500 mg tablets) in 24 hours, with at least 4 hours between doses. Less if you weigh under 50 kg or have liver problems. Can I take paracetamol and ibuprofen together? Yes, adults can take them together or alternate them, as they work differently. Stick to the maximum dose of each. Can I take ibuprofen for dengue fever? No. Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs increase bleeding risk in dengue. Use paracetamol for any fever until dengue is ruled out. What is mefenamic acid used for? Mainly period pain. The usual adult dose is 500 mg three times a day, taken with food. Is ibuprofen safe in pregnancy? Avoid it from 20 weeks of pregnancy unless a doctor advises. Paracetamol is usually the preferred painkiller in pregnancy. What should I do if I took too much paracetamol? Go to an emergency department straight away, even if you feel well. Liver damage may not show for a day or more, and early treatment works best. Which painkiller is best for toothache or period pain? Anti-inflammatories such as ibuprofen often work best, and combining ibuprofen with paracetamol is very effective, if NSAIDs are safe for you.

title: Frozen shoulder and shoulder pain (sakit bahu): stages, what helps, and when to see a doctor
desc: A shoulder that gets steadily more painful and stiff, until you can’t reach behind your back, is often frozen shoulder. Who gets it, why diabetes matters, what the evidence says about exercises, injections and surgery, and how to tell it from a rotator cuff problem.
headings: What is frozen shoulder, and who gets it? · Symptoms and stages · What helps · Other causes of shoulder pain (sakit bahu) · When to see a doctor
keywords: Guides Frozen shoulder Frozen shoulder Adhesive capsulitis Shoulder pain kencing manis gula hba1c kecemasan emergency a&e hospital aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Frozen shoulder affects about 2 to 5% of people, mostly aged 40 to 60, and more often women. Diabetes makes it about 5 times more likely. It causes pain, often worse at night, and stiffness in every direction, so it becomes hard to reach behind your back or put on a shirt. It usually goes through a painful freezing stage, a stiff frozen stage and a slow thawing stage, over 1 to 3 years. Some people keep a little stiffness. Keep the shoulder moving. Gentle exercises, painkillers, physiotherapy and a steroid injection in the early painful stage all help. In a large UK trial, surgery and manipulation weren’t clearly better than physiotherapy with a steroid injection, so they are usually kept for shoulders that don’t improve. The shoulder joint is surrounded by a capsule of tough tissue. In frozen shoulder, the capsule becomes inflamed, then thickens and tightens, leaving less room for the joint to move. The cause is often unclear. It is more likely if you: are aged 40 to 60 , especially if you are a woman have diabetes . About 1 in 8 people with diabetes get frozen shoulder, about 5 times the rate in other people, and it can be more stubborn. In Malaysia, 15.6% of adults have diabetes, and 2 in 5 of them don’t know it. If you have frozen shoulder, it is worth checking your blood sugar . have thyroid disease , heart disease or Parkinson’s disease have had your arm kept still after an injury, fracture or surgery, even a minor wrist or elbow injury in a sling or cast Between 2 and 5% of people develop frozen shoulder, and in up to 3 in 10 it later affects the other shoulder. Frozen shoulder causes a dull ache around the outer shoulder and upper arm, pain at night that disturbs sleep, and stiffness when moving the arm in any direction, even when someone else moves it for you. Everyday tasks such as fastening a bra, reaching behind your back or into a high cupboard become hard. Stage Usually lasts What happens Freezing 2 to 9 months Pain gradually builds, and movement starts to get worse Frozen 4 to 12 months Pain may ease, but the shoulder is very stiff Thawing 6 months to 2 years Movement slowly returns The whole process can take up to 3 years. These stages overlap, and recovery isn’t always complete: studies suggest many people regain most but not all of their movement, and people with diabetes are more likely to keep some stiffness. Diagnosis is usually made by examining the shoulder. An X-ray is often normal and is used to rule out other problems such as arthritis. An MRI isn’t usually needed. A doctor may do blood tests to check for diabetes or thyroid disease. Keep moving as much as you can, within your pain. Using a sling or resting the arm for long periods makes stiffness worse. Painkillers: paracetamol, then an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen if suitable. Heat: a heat pack for up to 20 minutes before exercises can help. Physiotherapy: usually for at least 6 weeks, with exercises to do at home. Steroid injection: an injection into the shoulder joint can ease pain and help movement, especially early on, in the first few months. Adding it to physiotherapy works better than physiotherapy alone. In people with diabetes, it can raise blood sugar for a few days, so check your levels. Two simple exercises (stop if the pain gets worse): Pendulum: hold a table with your good arm, bend forward and let the sore arm hang. Swing it gently back and forth, then in small circles, for 2 to 3 minutes, several times a day. Wall climb: face a wall and walk your fingers up it as high as you can without too much pain. Hold for 15 to 30 seconds, and repeat 2 to 4 times. If it doesn’t improve: options include a large-volume injection to stretch the joint (hydrodilatation), which helps mainly in the short term, manipulation under anaesthetic , and keyhole surgery to release the tight capsule. In the UK FROST trial of 503 people, published in The Lancet in 2020, surgery, manipulation and physiotherapy with a steroid injection all gave similar results at a year, and surgery had more serious complications. So these are usually kept for shoulders that remain painful and stiff despite other treatment. Be careful with forceful “cracking” or deep massage. Malaysian specialists warn that forcing a stiff shoulder can cause fractures in weak bones or tear the tendons. See a doctor first. Gentle, regular exercises help keep the shoulder moving while it recovers. Cause Typical signs Rotator cuff problems Pain when lifting the arm out to the side or overhead, weakness, night pain. Movement is usually fine if someone else moves your arm. Most improve with exercises over weeks to months, without surgery Calcific tendinopathy Sudden, severe shoulder pain from calcium deposits in a tendon Arthritis Pain with activity, grinding, stiffness, usually in older adults. Shows on X-ray A problem in the neck Pain spreading from the neck into the shoulder and arm, sometimes with tingling. See our guide to slipped discs Call 999 if arm or shoulder pain comes with chest pain or tightness, breathlessness or sweating, as it could be a heart attack . Don’t drive yourself. Go to an emergency department if you can’t move your arm after an injury, the shoulder has changed shape, or the arm is numb, hot or cold. Don’t try to put a dislocated shoulder back yourself. shoulder pain that is getting worse, or hasn’t improved after 2 weeks you can’t move your arm normally, or pain wakes you at night both shoulders are affected, or you have a fever you have diabetes and a stiff shoulder After an injury or surgery, ask when you can start gentle shoulder exercises, to help prevent stiffness. What are the first signs of frozen shoulder? Gradually worsening shoulder pain, often at night, followed by stiffness that makes it hard to reach behind your back or overhead. How long does frozen shoulder last? Usually 1 to 3 years, through freezing, frozen and thawing stages. Treatment can ease pain during this time. Who gets frozen shoulder? Mostly people aged 40 to 60, more often women. People with diabetes or thyroid disease, or whose arm has been kept still after an injury, are at higher risk. Does frozen shoulder go away on its own? It usually improves slowly over time, but some people keep some stiffness. Exercises, physiotherapy and injections can help. Should I rest a frozen shoulder? No. Keep moving it gently, within your pain. Long periods of rest make stiffness worse. Does a steroid injection help frozen shoulder? Yes, particularly in the early, painful stage. It works better alongside physiotherapy. Do I need surgery for frozen shoulder? Most people don’t. A large trial found surgery wasn’t clearly better than physiotherapy with a steroid injection, so it is kept for shoulders that don’t improve. Can shoulder pain be a heart attack? Yes. Call 999 if arm or shoulder pain comes with chest pain or tightness, breathlessness or sweating.

title: Low blood pressure (darah rendah): normal readings, symptoms, causes and what to do
desc: A blood pressure below 90/60 is usually harmless if you feel well. But if you feel dizzy or faint when you stand up, there may be a cause worth finding. What counts as low, why it happens, what helps, and when low blood pressure is an emergency.
headings: What is a low blood pressure reading? (Bacaan tekanan darah rendah) · Symptoms · Causes (punca darah rendah) · What helps (cara menaikkan tekanan darah rendah) · Older adults and falls · When to get help
keywords: Heart & diabetes Low blood pressure Hypotension Tekanan darah rendah Orthostatic hypotension kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah kesihatan mental depression anxiety stress kemurungan mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Low blood pressure generally means below 90/60 mmHg. If you feel well, it usually needs no treatment. Symptoms include dizziness or light-headedness, blurred vision, nausea, weakness and fainting, especially on standing up. Common causes are dehydration, medicines for blood pressure, depression or Parkinson’s disease, pregnancy, and heat. Sudden low blood pressure can come from bleeding or severe infection. Stand up slowly, drink more water, eat smaller meals, avoid standing for long, and don’t stop prescribed medicines on your own. Call 999 for fainting with chest pain, or cold, clammy, pale skin with fast breathing, confusion or heavy bleeding, which can mean shock. Category Top number (systolic) Bottom number (diastolic) Low Below 90 Below 60 Optimal Below 120 Below 80 Normal 120 to 129 80 to 84 The optimal and normal bands come from Malaysia’s Clinical Practice Guidelines on hypertension, which set no lower limit. The “below 90/60” figure is the commonly used definition of low blood pressure. For high readings and how to measure at home, see our guides to high blood pressure and checking your blood pressure at home . Low blood pressure often isn’t a problem. Fit people and those with a family history of low blood pressure may naturally have low readings and feel completely well. “Darah rendah” or “kurang darah”? People sometimes mix these up because the symptoms overlap. Darah rendah means low blood pressure. Kurang darah means anaemia, a low level of haemoglobin in the blood. They are different conditions with different treatments. See our guide to anaemia . dizziness or light-headedness (see our guide to vertigo and dizziness ) blurred vision feeling sick weakness and tiredness headache or palpitations confusion fainting Types of low blood pressure: Postural (orthostatic) hypotension: blood pressure falls when you stand up, by at least 20 points on the top number or 10 on the bottom within 3 minutes. It causes dizziness on standing and becomes more common with age. After meals (postprandial): a fall in blood pressure within 2 hours of eating, mostly in older people. Vasovagal fainting: a sudden drop triggered by heat, standing for a long time, pain, stress or the sight of blood, often with nausea, sweating, paleness and tunnel vision first. Dehydration , from hot weather, not drinking enough, vomiting or diarrhoea. See our guide to food poisoning and rehydration . Medicines , including blood pressure tablets, water tablets (diuretics), alpha-blockers for the prostate, and some medicines for depression or Parkinson’s disease Pregnancy: blood pressure normally dips in the first half of pregnancy, and usually needs no treatment. Lying on your side can help. Fainting in early pregnancy with pain or bleeding needs urgent care. See our guide to early pregnancy warning signs . Long periods of bed rest Diabetes affecting the nerves that control blood pressure, and Parkinson’s disease Heart problems , such as a heart attack or heart failure Anaemia , or blood loss from an injury or inside the body Adrenal gland problems (Addison’s disease) Severe infection (sepsis) or a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) Hot weather: during the 2026 hot spell, the Ministry of Health advised people to avoid being outdoors from 11 am to 4 pm, drink at least 8 glasses of water and limit caffeinated drinks. Fasting: older people who fast in Ramadan should review their blood pressure medicines with a doctor beforehand, rehydrate well between iftar and sahur, and take care when standing up. Stand up slowly , especially first thing in the morning. Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute first. Drink more water through the day, unless you have been told to limit fluids. Eat smaller, more frequent meals , with fewer heavy carbohydrates, if you feel dizzy after eating. Avoid standing still for long , hot baths, and too much alcohol. Tensing your legs, crossing them or squeezing your thighs helps push blood back up. Support stockings may help some people. Ask a doctor first. Raising the head of your bed slightly can help with dizziness in the morning. More salt helps some people, but only on a doctor’s advice, especially if you have heart or kidney disease or high blood pressure. If you feel faint: lie down and raise your legs, or sit with your head between your knees, until you feel better. Stand up slowly afterwards. Medicines: if a medicine may be the cause, your doctor may change it. Don’t stop prescribed medicines by yourself. Medicines to raise blood pressure are rarely needed. Food: there is no good evidence that particular foods, such as goat meat, cure low blood pressure. Regular meals and enough fluids matter more. Dizziness on standing is more common with age and raises the risk of falls. Postural hypotension becomes more common with age and is linked to falls, even in people without symptoms. If an older relative feels dizzy on standing, or has had a fall, ask a doctor to check their blood pressure lying down and then standing, and to review their medicines. Call 999 or go to an emergency department if someone: faints and has chest pain , an irregular heartbeat, a seizure, or doesn’t wake within a minute faints during exercise or while lying down has pale, cold, clammy skin with fast, shallow breathing , a weak pulse, or confusion or restlessness. These are signs of shock . Lay them down with their legs raised. has black, tarry stools , heavy bleeding or is vomiting blood has signs of severe dehydration or infection, such as blotchy skin, drowsiness or a high fever See a doctor if you often feel dizzy or faint, have fallen, or your low readings are new or come with symptoms. A doctor can check your blood pressure lying and standing, and may arrange blood tests and a heart tracing (ECG). See our guide on clinic or emergency department . What is considered low blood pressure? Generally below 90/60 mmHg. If you feel well, it usually isn’t a problem and needs no treatment. What are the symptoms of low blood pressure? Dizziness, light-headedness, blurred vision, nausea, weakness and fainting, particularly on standing up. What causes low blood pressure? Common causes are dehydration, some medicines, pregnancy, heat and long bed rest. Heart problems, bleeding and severe infections can also cause it. Is darah rendah the same as kurang darah? No. Darah rendah means low blood pressure. Kurang darah means anaemia, or low haemoglobin. They are different conditions. How can I raise low blood pressure quickly? If you feel faint, lie down and raise your legs, or sit with your head between your knees. Drink water, and stand up slowly afterwards. What should I eat for low blood pressure? Regular, smaller meals and enough fluids help most. No particular food is proven to cure it. Check with a doctor before adding extra salt. Is low blood pressure dangerous? Usually not, but fainting can cause injuries, and sudden low blood pressure with chest pain, confusion, or cold, clammy skin is an emergency. Why do I feel dizzy when I stand up? Blood pressure can drop briefly on standing, which is called postural hypotension. It is common with dehydration, some medicines and older age.

title: Mouth ulcers (ulser mulut) and cold sores: causes, what helps, and when to see a doctor
desc: Most mouth ulcers heal within 2 weeks, and cold sores within about 10 days. What causes them, what eases the pain, when ulcers that keep coming back need blood tests, and why an ulcer that won’t heal should always be checked for mouth cancer, especially if you smoke or chew sirih.
headings: Mouth ulcers (ulser mulut) · What helps (cara hilangkan ulser mulut) · When an ulcer could be mouth cancer · Cold sores · Mouth sores in children · When to see a doctor or dentist
keywords: Guides Mouth ulcers and cold sores Aphthous stomatitis Ulser mulut Herpes labialis klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Mouth ulcers are usually round and white or yellow, on the inside of the cheeks, lips or tongue. They clear in 1 to 2 weeks and aren’t contagious. Triggers include biting your cheek, braces, sharp teeth, stress, tiredness, hormonal changes and some foods. Ulcers that keep coming back can be a sign of low iron, vitamin B12 or folate, or of bowel conditions, and are worth a blood test. A mouth ulcer that hasn’t healed in 2 to 3 weeks must be checked by a dentist or doctor. In Malaysia, more than 60% of mouth cancers are found late. Cold sores are caused by the herpes simplex virus. Antiviral cream works best at the first tingle. Keep them away from newborn babies and your eyes. Common mouth ulcers (recurrent aphthous stomatitis) are shallow, round sores with a white or yellow centre and a red edge, on the inside of the cheeks or lips, or under the tongue. Most are small and heal within 10 to 14 days. Larger ones can take weeks and may scar. They often run in families. Common triggers (punca ulser mulut): biting your cheek, sharp teeth, braces or dentures that rub, hard brushing, or burns from hot food stress, tiredness and hormonal changes, such as around periods stopping smoking certain foods in some people, such as chocolate, coffee, peanuts, cheese and tomatoes toothpaste containing sodium lauryl sulphate (SLS). Switching to SLS-free toothpaste may help, but the evidence is limited. If ulcers keep coming back, see a doctor. Possible causes include low iron, folate or vitamin B12, coeliac disease, Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, Behçet’s disease, a weakened immune system, and some medicines, such as NSAIDs and nicorandil. See our guides to anaemia and blood tests . Use a soft toothbrush , and avoid spicy, salty, sour, crunchy or very hot food until it heals. Have cool drinks through a straw, and soft foods. Rinse with warm salt water (half a teaspoon in a glass of warm water, then spit it out). This is a traditional, low-risk remedy, although it hasn’t been well studied. Ask a pharmacist about an antiseptic mouthwash (such as alcohol-free chlorhexidine), a numbing gel or spray , a protective paste, or low-strength steroid lozenges. A dentist or doctor can prescribe stronger steroid treatments for severe or frequent ulcers. Honey applied to ulcers shortened healing in some small studies, but it won’t suit everyone. Don’t give honey to babies under 1. Numbing gels and children: the US Food and Drug Administration warns that benzocaine, a numbing ingredient in some gels, can rarely cause a dangerous blood problem (methaemoglobinaemia), and young children are at particular risk. Ask a pharmacist before using any numbing product on a child. See a dentist or doctor if an ulcer hasn’t healed in 2 weeks , and don’t leave it beyond 3 weeks. Also get checked for: a red or white patch in the mouth a lump in the mouth, on the lip or in the neck numbness in the mouth or lips, or loose teeth with no obvious reason persistent pain, difficulty swallowing or speaking, or a hoarse voice Most of these aren’t cancer, but mouth cancer is much easier to treat when found early. According to the Ministry of Health’s 2025 oral health guideline, Malaysia had 742 new cases and 403 deaths in 2020, and more than 60% are detected late . It is more common in people of Indian origin and among indigenous communities in Sabah and Sarawak. Main risk factors: smoking, chewing betel quid ( sirih ) or tobacco, alcohol, and HPV infection. Betel quid with tobacco raises the risk 3 to 8 times. Regular dental checks can pick up early changes. Government dental clinics examine new patients aged 18 and over for signs of mouth cancer. Cold sores are small blisters on or around the lips, usually caused by the herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) . Most people catch it in childhood, and the virus stays in the body for life, sometimes flaring up. They start with tingling, itching or burning , then blisters form within about 2 days, burst, scab over and heal in about 10 days. Triggers include illness, sun, stress and periods. Contagious from the first tingle until fully healed. Avoid kissing and oral sex, and don’t share cups, towels or lip balm. Treatment: antiviral cream (such as aciclovir) from a pharmacy works best if started at the first tingle. A doctor can prescribe antiviral tablets for large, painful or frequent cold sores. Lip balm with SPF 15 or more can help prevent sun-triggered ones. Important: Never kiss a newborn baby if you have a cold sore , and wash your hands. Herpes in a young baby can be very dangerous. A baby with a fever of 38°C or more, poor feeding or sores needs urgent care. Keep it away from your eyes. See a doctor urgently for eye pain, redness, blurred vision or sensitivity to light. See a doctor if a cold sore hasn’t healed after 10 days, or you have a weakened immune system. Sores on the genitals have other causes. See our guide to STI testing . Hand, foot and mouth disease: sores in the mouth with a rash on the hands and feet. See our HFMD guide . Herpes gingivostomatitis: a first infection with the cold sore virus, usually at ages 1 to 5, causing fever, swollen, bleeding gums and many mouth sores. It usually clears in about 2 weeks. A doctor can advise whether antiviral treatment is worthwhile. The main risk is dehydration , as children refuse to drink because of the pain. Offer cold drinks, ice lollies and oral rehydration fluid, and give paracetamol for pain. Fluids matter more than food. See a doctor urgently if your child refuses all drinks, has far fewer wet nappies or dark urine, or is hard to wake. See our guide to fever in children . an ulcer lasting more than 2 to 3 weeks ulcers that keep coming back, are unusually large, or are spreading or near the throat ulcers that bleed or become redder and more painful sores on the skin or genitals as well as in the mouth, or swollen joints a sharp tooth, brace or denture that keeps rubbing What causes mouth ulcers? Usually minor injury, such as biting your cheek or braces, stress, tiredness, hormonal changes or some foods. Ulcers that keep returning can be linked to low iron, B12 or folate. How long do mouth ulcers last? Most heal within 1 to 2 weeks. See a dentist or doctor if one hasn’t healed after 2 to 3 weeks. How can I get rid of a mouth ulcer quickly? There is no instant cure, but a soft toothbrush, avoiding spicy or sour food, an antiseptic mouthwash, a numbing gel from a pharmacy and salt-water rinses can ease it while it heals. Which vitamins help mouth ulcers? If you are low in iron, vitamin B12 or folate, treating that may reduce ulcers. Ask a doctor for a blood test rather than guessing. Are mouth ulcers contagious? No, ordinary mouth ulcers aren’t contagious. Cold sores are. Can a mouth ulcer be cancer? Most aren’t, but an ulcer that doesn’t heal in 2 to 3 weeks, especially if you smoke, drink or chew sirih, must be checked. What is the difference between a mouth ulcer and a cold sore? Mouth ulcers are inside the mouth and aren’t contagious. Cold sores are blisters on or around the lips, caused by a virus, and are contagious. How do I treat a cold sore? Use antiviral cream at the first tingle. A doctor can prescribe tablets for severe or frequent cold sores. Avoid kissing babies until it has fully healed.

title: Tuberculosis (TB, tibi, batuk kering) in Malaysia: symptoms, tests, treatment and latent TB
desc: Malaysia records more than 26,000 TB cases a year. The symptoms to look out for, how TB spreads and doesn’t, the tests, why the 6-month treatment must be finished, what latent TB means, and what to do if someone close to you has it.
headings: TB in Malaysia · How TB spreads, and who is at risk · Symptoms of TB · Tests for TB · Treatment · Latent TB · If someone close to you has TB
keywords: Prevention Tuberculosis (TB) Tuberculosis Tibi Latent tuberculosis kencing manis gula hba1c vaksin suntikan jab immunisation klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Malaysia recorded 26,183 TB cases and 2,580 deaths in 2024. About 85% of cases are in Malaysians, and Sabah, Selangor and Sarawak have the most. See a doctor for a cough lasting more than 2 weeks, especially with fever, night sweats, weight loss or coughing up blood. TB spreads through the air during close, repeated contact. It doesn’t spread through food, drink, handshakes or kissing. Standard treatment is 6 months of daily tablets. Stopping early can lead to relapse and drug-resistant TB. Most people stop being infectious after about 2 weeks of effective treatment. Latent TB means you carry the bacteria without being ill or infectious. Close contacts should be checked, and some are offered preventive treatment. In 2024 , Malaysia reported 26,183 cases and 2,580 deaths , about 77 cases per 100,000 people. The government aims to eliminate TB by 2035. Up to 6 June 2026 , there were 11,257 cases, 4.4% more than the same period in 2025. The Health Minister attributed the rise to more active case-finding. In February 2026, a cluster of 37 cases in Kota Tinggi, Johor , including students, led to more than 800 contacts being screened and a wave of public concern. In the first weeks of 2026, Sabah had the most cases, followed by Selangor, Sarawak, Johor and Kuala Lumpur. About 85% of cases are in Malaysians , and about 15% in foreigners. Health officials call it a disease of poverty and crowding, and urge people not to shun patients. TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis . Someone with active TB in the lungs releases it into the air when they cough, sneeze or speak. It spreads more slowly than flu or COVID-19, usually through prolonged, repeated contact in shared indoor air, such as at home, in hostels or in crowded workplaces. TB doesn’t spread through food or drink, toothbrushes, handshakes or kissing, and only people with active TB can pass it on. Higher risk: people with diabetes , HIV, poor nutrition, those who smoke or drink heavily, close contacts of someone with TB, and young children. Diabetes matters especially in Malaysia: in a Kelantan study, 28% of TB patients had diabetes, and they were about 3 times more likely to have poor treatment outcomes. That is why every TB patient is screened for diabetes and HIV. See our guide to blood sugar . a cough lasting more than 2 weeks coughing up blood or phlegm fever and night sweats loss of appetite and weight loss tiredness and chest pain TB can also affect other parts of the body, causing swollen glands, joint or back pain, or headaches and confusion if it reaches the brain. In children, it may show as poor weight gain and growth. Some people with TB have few or no symptoms but can still spread it. For other causes of a lingering cough, see our guide to a cough that won’t go away . Sputum tests: two or more samples of phlegm, ideally including an early-morning one, are examined and tested. Molecular tests (Xpert Ultra) used in Ministry of Health facilities find TB quickly and detect some drug resistance. Chest X-ray Culture and drug-sensitivity tests show which medicines will work. Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) and IGRA blood test show whether you have been infected. They can’t tell latent from active TB, and may stay negative in the first 8 weeks after exposure. TB is a notifiable disease under the Prevention and Control of Infectious Diseases Act 1988, so doctors must report cases to the health office, which then traces close contacts. Sputum tests, chest X-rays and blood tests are used to find TB. Under Malaysia’s clinical practice guideline, standard treatment for lung TB takes 6 months : First 2 months: four medicines daily (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol) Next 4 months: two medicines daily (isoniazid and rifampicin) TB of the brain, bones or joints needs longer treatment. Drug-resistant TB can take up to 2 years. Directly observed treatment (DOT): a health worker, trained family member or volunteer watches you take your medicines. Video DOT is available in some places. Finish the full course , even when you feel better. Many people feel well after a few weeks, but stopping early can cause relapse and drug-resistant TB. Researchers report that a substantial share of Malaysian patients don’t complete treatment. Side effects: orange or red urine and tears are harmless. See a doctor quickly for yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, vomiting, rash, numbness, or changes in your vision. Cost: TB medicines are provided free at government health facilities. Infectiousness: most people stop being infectious after about 2 weeks of effective treatment, but your doctor will decide when it is safe to return to work or school. About a quarter of people worldwide have been infected with TB bacteria. In latent TB , the bacteria are inactive: you feel well, you can’t pass it on, and your chest X-ray is usually normal.
