About 5 to 10% go on to develop active TB, most often in the first few years, and the risk is higher with a weak immune system, diabetes, or in young children. Preventive treatment greatly lowers the risk. Malaysia’s guideline recommends it for groups such as household contacts, people with HIV, people on dialysis or some immune-suppressing medicines, and young children, usually with a 3-month course. Children under 5 who have been in contact with TB are at highest risk and should be checked promptly. Go for screening when the health office contacts you, even if you feel well. Tests may be repeated after 8 weeks. Keep rooms well ventilated, with windows open and fans on. The person with TB should cover coughs and wear a mask, especially in the first weeks of treatment. Support them to finish treatment. People with TB aren’t dangerous once treated, and stigma stops people from coming forward. The Ministry of Health also advises wearing a mask if you have a cough or are in crowded places. BCG vaccine: Malaysian babies get BCG at birth. It protects young children against severe forms of TB, such as TB meningitis. Its protection against lung TB in adults is uncertain, so vaccinated people can still get TB. See our baby vaccination schedule . What are the symptoms of TB? A cough lasting more than 2 weeks, coughing up blood, fever, night sweats, loss of appetite and weight loss. How does TB spread? Through the air when someone with active lung TB coughs, sneezes or speaks, usually after prolonged contact. Not through food, drink, handshakes or kissing. Is TB curable? Yes. Standard TB is cured with 6 months of medicines, as long as the full course is finished. How long is TB treatment? Usually 6 months for lung TB: four medicines for 2 months, then two medicines for 4 months. Drug-resistant TB can take up to 2 years. When is someone with TB no longer infectious? Usually after about 2 weeks of effective treatment, but a doctor decides when it is safe to return to work or school. Is TB treatment free in Malaysia? TB medicines are provided free at government health facilities. Check with the clinic about other charges. What is latent TB? An inactive infection with no symptoms. You can’t spread it, but it can turn into active TB, so some people are offered preventive treatment. Does the BCG vaccine prevent TB? It protects young children from severe TB, but its protection against lung TB in adults is uncertain.

title: Constipation (sembelit): causes, what helps, laxatives, and warning signs
desc: Constipation affects about 1 in 10 Malaysians. What counts as constipation, the foods and habits with the best evidence, how the different laxatives work and how quickly, what to do for babies, children and in pregnancy, and the warning signs not to ignore.
headings: What is constipation? · Common causes · What helps (cara atasi sembelit) · Laxatives (ubat sembelit) · Babies and children (sembelit bayi dan kanak-kanak) · Constipation in pregnancy · When to see a doctor
keywords: Guides Constipation (sembelit) Constipation Sembelit Laxatives kencing manis gula hba1c payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical
body: Constipation usually means fewer than 3 bowel movements a week, or hard stools, straining or a feeling of not emptying. About 1 in 10 Malaysian adults in primary care are affected. Malaysia recommends 20 to 30 g of fibre a day, but most adults fall short. Add fibre gradually with enough water. Kiwifruit, psyllium and prunes have good evidence. Regular exercise and a set toilet time help too. Macrogol (PEG) and psyllium are well-supported laxatives. Stimulant laxatives such as senna and bisacodyl work within 6 to 12 hours and are for short-term use. Check with a doctor if you need one for more than a week. See a doctor for blood in your stool, weight loss, anaemia, a new change in bowel habit after 50, or a family history of bowel cancer. Severe tummy pain with no wind or stool is an emergency. Everyone’s bowel habit is different. Doctors usually call it constipation if, for several weeks, you have: fewer than 3 bowel movements a week hard or lumpy stools straining, or a feeling of not emptying fully or of something blocking the way Worldwide, about 9 to 20% of people are affected, and it is about twice as common in women. Malaysian studies have found it in about 11% of adults attending primary care, and 15% of older clinic patients. not eating enough fibre or drinking enough fluids not moving enough, or long periods of sitting or bed rest ignoring the urge to go, or a change in routine, such as travel or shift work stress, and irritable bowel syndrome pregnancy and older age Medicines , including iron tablets, opioid painkillers such as codeine, some antacids, some antidepressants and calcium channel blockers conditions such as diabetes, an underactive thyroid and Parkinson’s disease Straining can cause piles (buasir) and small tears around the anus. Fibre: Malaysia’s recommended intake is 20 to 30 g a day, but most adults eat less, and Malaysians average under 2 servings each of fruit and vegetables a day. Increase it gradually over a few weeks to avoid bloating. Foods with the best evidence: a 2025 British Dietetic Association guideline found good support for kiwifruit (2 to 3 a day for at least 4 weeks), psyllium fibre, and rye bread. Prunes are also useful. It found less support for a general “high-fibre diet” for long-term constipation, so the type of fibre matters. Fluids: drink about 1.5 to 2 litres a day. Move more: aim for 150 minutes of activity a week. Toilet routine: go when you feel the urge, try after breakfast, and don’t rush. Put your feet on a low stool so your knees are above your hips. Most Malaysians eat fewer than the recommended servings of fruit and vegetables. Type Examples How long to work Notes Bulk-forming Ispaghula (psyllium) Up to 3 days Take with plenty of water. A good first choice Osmotic Macrogol (PEG), lactulose 2 to 3 days Draw water into the bowel. Macrogol has strong evidence Stimulant Senna, bisacodyl 6 to 12 hours Make the bowel contract. Can cause cramps. Mainly for short-term use Softener Docusate 12 hours to 3 days Softens the stool Enemas Sodium citrate 5 to 15 minutes For severe constipation, on advice See a doctor if pharmacy laxatives haven’t helped after 3 days, and don’t use them for more than 7 days without advice. At recommended doses, stimulant laxatives are unlikely to damage the bowel, but overuse can cause dehydration and low potassium. Be careful with “detox” teas and slimming products. In 2024 and 2025, Singapore’s food authority found the undeclared laxative sennosides in slimming products made in Malaysia, and the Ministry of Health has warned about unregistered slimming products with hidden drugs. These can cause dehydration and low potassium. Babies: breastfed babies may go after every feed or only once a week, and both can be normal if the stool is soft. Bottle-fed babies usually go every 1 to 3 days. If you think a baby under 1 is constipated, see a doctor. Don’t give laxatives or enemas without medical advice. Children: signs are fewer than 3 stools a week, hard pellets, pain, or soiling their underwear. Pain makes them hold back, which makes it worse. Encourage them to sit on the toilet after meals with their feet supported, and give fibre and fluids. Children often need macrogol from a doctor, sometimes for several months. See a GP early. See a doctor urgently if a newborn didn’t pass stool in the first 48 hours, if constipation began in the first weeks of life, or if there is a swollen tummy with vomiting, or leg weakness. Try fibre, fluids and activity first. If needed, bulk-forming laxatives, then lactulose or macrogol, are preferred, as they aren’t absorbed. Senna is used only if those don’t work. Iron tablets can make constipation worse, so ask if a different preparation may help. See our pregnancy guide . See a doctor if you have constipation with: blood in your stool , or dark stools unexplained weight loss or anaemia a new, lasting change in your bowel habit, especially from age 50 a family history of bowel cancer a lump in your tummy, or constipation that doesn’t improve after several weeks The Ministry of Health’s bowel cancer guideline advises referral for a colonoscopy when such symptoms don’t resolve in 4 to 6 weeks. See our guide to bowel cancer screening . Go to an emergency department for severe tummy pain with a swollen tummy, vomiting, and no wind or stool passing, which can mean a blocked bowel. Don’t eat or drink. See our guide to stomach pain . Older people can develop faecal impaction, where a hard mass of stool blocks the bowel. It can cause confusion, difficulty passing urine, poor appetite, and watery leakage that looks like diarrhoea. Don’t give anti-diarrhoea medicine. See a doctor. What is sembelit in English? Sembelit is constipation: passing stools less often than usual, or hard stools that are difficult to pass. How often should I go to the toilet? It varies from person to person. Fewer than 3 times a week, with hard stools or straining, usually counts as constipation. What foods help constipation? Kiwifruit, prunes, psyllium fibre, and fruit, vegetables and wholegrains generally. Increase fibre gradually and drink enough water. What is the best laxative? Psyllium and macrogol have good evidence for regular use. Stimulant laxatives such as senna or bisacodyl work faster and are mainly for short-term use. Are laxatives safe? Yes, at the recommended dose for short periods. Long-term or heavy use should be supervised by a doctor. Don’t use them for weight loss. How do I help my constipated child? Give fibre and fluids, and have them sit on the toilet after meals with their feet supported. See a GP early, as children often need a laxative for some months. Is constipation in pregnancy normal? Yes, it is common. Try fibre and fluids first, then ask about bulk-forming laxatives, lactulose or macrogol. When is constipation serious? With blood in the stool, weight loss, anaemia, a new change in bowel habit after 50, or severe pain with vomiting and no wind.

title: Enlarged prostate and the PSA test: symptoms, treatment and prostate cancer screening in Malaysia
desc: Getting up at night to pass urine, a weak stream and dribbling are common in men over 50, and are often caused by an enlarged prostate. What helps, how medicines and surgery compare, what a PSA test can and can’t tell you, and what Malaysian men should know about prostate cancer.
headings: What is an enlarged prostate? · Symptoms · How it is checked · Treatment · The PSA test · Prostate cancer in Malaysia
keywords: Guides Enlarged prostate and PSA test Benign prostatic hyperplasia Prostate-specific antigen Prostate cancer kencing manis gula hba1c kecemasan emergency a&e hospital saringan check-up checkup medical aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Enlarged prostate symptoms include a weak or stop-start stream, straining, dribbling, needing to go often or urgently, and getting up at night. Being suddenly unable to pass urine is an emergency. Blood in the urine should be checked promptly. Mild symptoms can be managed with lifestyle changes. Alpha-blockers work within days, and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors shrink the prostate over 6 months or more. The PSA blood test can pick up prostate cancer early, but a raised PSA doesn’t always mean cancer, and screening has benefits and harms. Men from 50, or 45 with a family history, should discuss it with their doctor. Prostate cancer is the third most common cancer in Malaysian men, and 63% of cases with staging are found late. The prostate sits just below the bladder, around the tube that carries urine out (the urethra). As men age, it often grows and squeezes the urethra, which makes it harder to pass urine. This is called benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) . Benign means it isn’t cancer. In Malaysia: the National Health and Morbidity Survey 2019 found that 16.3% of men aged 40 and over had probable BPH with moderate to severe symptoms, rising from 10.5% at 40 to 44 to 33.4% at 75 and over. difficulty starting to pass urine, and straining a weak or stop-start stream dribbling at the end a feeling that the bladder hasn’t emptied ( kencing tak lawas ) needing to go often or urgently getting up at night to pass urine ( kencing malam ) Getting up at night has other causes too, such as drinking late in the evening, alcohol, caffeine, diuretics, diabetes, heart failure and sleep apnoea. See also our guide to urinary tract infections . Go to an emergency department if you can’t pass urine at all , especially with lower tummy pain. This is acute urinary retention, and needs a catheter. Blood in the urine, fever with urinary symptoms, or side or back pain also need prompt attention. Untreated BPH can lead to infections, bladder stones and kidney damage. A doctor will ask about your symptoms, sometimes using a short score (the International Prostate Symptom Score) and a 3-day bladder diary, and may do: a rectal examination with a gloved finger to feel the prostate a urine test for infection and blood blood tests for kidney function and PSA, if needed a urine flow test and an ultrasound of the bladder after passing urine Lifestyle changes, for mild symptoms: Drink less in the 2 hours before bed, but don’t cut down fluids too much overall. Limit caffeine and alcohol. Try “double voiding”: pass urine, wait a moment, then try again. Treat constipation. See our guide to constipation . Avoid cold remedies containing decongestants or antihistamines, which can make symptoms worse. Medicines: Type How it works Notes Alpha-blockers (such as tamsulosin) Relax the muscle around the urethra. Work within days Can cause dizziness on standing and ejaculation changes. Tell your eye surgeon before cataract surgery 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) Shrink the prostate over at least 6 months Reduce the risk of retention and surgery. Can lower libido. They halve your PSA reading, so tell your doctor Combination Both of the above For larger prostates. More effective, with more side effects Surgery and procedures: for severe symptoms, or complications such as retention. Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) is the standard operation, removing the central part of the prostate through the urethra. Other options include laser treatment, water vapour therapy and microwave treatment, some of which are offered in Malaysian private hospitals. After TURP, most men have dry orgasms (retrograde ejaculation), and some have new erection problems. Ask your surgeon about the risks of each option. PSA (prostate-specific antigen) is a protein made by the prostate, measured with a blood test. A raised level can mean prostate cancer, but also BPH, a urine infection or inflammation. It isn’t a cancer test by itself. Before the test, for 48 hours, avoid: ejaculation, vigorous exercise, and long cycling. Wait 4 to 6 weeks after a urine infection. You can eat normally. What screening can and can’t do: The large European ERSPC trial found that, after 23 years, PSA screening cut prostate cancer deaths by 13%. About 1 death was prevented for every 456 men invited. But many men with a raised PSA don’t have cancer: only about a quarter had it on biopsy. Screening can also find slow-growing cancers that would never cause harm, leading to unnecessary treatment. That is why guidelines recommend an informed choice , not automatic testing. The US task force advises men aged 55 to 69 to decide individually, and not to screen from 70. European urology guidelines suggest offering a test to informed men from 50 , or from 45 with a family history. Some Malaysian urologists recommend yearly tests from these ages. If your PSA is raised, it may be repeated, and you may have an MRI before deciding on a biopsy. A raised PSA doesn’t always mean cancer, so results need explaining by a doctor. It is the third most common cancer in Malaysian men , with 6,441 cases recorded from 2017 to 2021, up from 4,189 in the previous five years, according to the National Cancer Registry. Among cases with staging, 63.3% were found at a late stage . Lifetime risk is highest in Chinese men (1 in 50), then Indian (1 in 83) and Malay men (1 in 125). Early prostate cancer often causes no symptoms . Advanced cancer can cause bone pain, especially in the back, along with weight loss and tiredness. Not every prostate cancer needs treatment straight away. Low-risk cancers can be watched closely with PSA tests and MRI scans ( active surveillance ), with treatment if they grow. The PERKESO free health screening doesn’t appear to include PSA as a standard test, so check what your package covers. See our guide to free health screening . What are the symptoms of an enlarged prostate? A weak or stop-start stream, straining, dribbling, needing to go often or urgently, and getting up at night to pass urine. Is an enlarged prostate cancer? No, BPH isn’t cancer. But prostate cancer can cause similar symptoms, so it should be checked. What should I do if I can’t pass urine? Go to an emergency department. Sudden inability to pass urine needs a catheter. What is a normal PSA level? It varies with age, and there is no single safe number. A doctor interprets it alongside your age, examination and other factors. At what age should men have a PSA test? European guidelines suggest discussing it from 50, or from 45 with a family history. It is an informed choice, not an automatic test. Does a high PSA mean I have cancer? Not necessarily. BPH, infection, recent ejaculation or cycling can raise PSA. Only about a quarter of men with a raised PSA in a large trial had cancer on biopsy. Will prostate surgery affect my sex life? After TURP, most men have dry orgasms, and some have erection problems. Discuss risks of each option with your surgeon. Why do I keep waking up at night to pass urine? An enlarged prostate is one cause. Others include evening drinks, caffeine, diabetes, heart failure and sleep apnoea.

title: Anaemia and iron deficiency (kurang darah): symptoms, tests, iron tablets and what to eat
desc: About 3 in 10 Malaysian women of reproductive age have anaemia. How it feels, what your haemoglobin and ferritin mean, why men and older women need their bowel checked, how to take iron tablets properly, and which Malaysian foods are rich in iron.
headings: What is anaemia? · Symptoms · Causes · Tests · Iron tablets (ubat tambah darah) · Iron-rich foods · Pregnancy and children · When to see a doctor
keywords: Guides Anaemia and iron deficiency Anaemia Iron deficiency Kurang darah darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Anaemia means haemoglobin below 13 g/dL in men, 12 g/dL in non-pregnant women, or 11 g/dL in pregnancy. About 3 in 10 Malaysian women aged 15 to 49 are affected. Common symptoms are tiredness, breathlessness, a fast heartbeat, pale skin and headaches. Iron deficiency is the most common cause, often from heavy periods or pregnancy. Men and women past the menopause with iron deficiency need their stomach and bowel checked. Get tested before taking iron. Thalassaemia trait causes similar blood results, and needs different advice. Take iron tablets once a day or on alternate days, away from tea, coffee and milk, and keep them out of children’s reach. An iron overdose can be fatal for children. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which carries oxygen. In anaemia, haemoglobin (Hb) is too low. The World Health Organization’s cut-offs are: Group Anaemia if haemoglobin is below Men 13 g/dL Non-pregnant women 12 g/dL Pregnant women 11 g/dL (10.5 g/dL in the second trimester) In Malaysia, national health surveys have found anaemia in 21.3% of the population in 2019, including about 3 in 10 women aged 15 to 49 , about 19% of pregnant women in 2022, and about a third of people aged 60 and over. “Kurang darah” isn’t the same as “darah rendah”. Darah rendah means low blood pressure. See our guide to low blood pressure . tiredness and lack of energy shortness of breath, especially on exertion a fast or pounding heartbeat pale skin headaches and dizziness less commonly: brittle nails, hair loss, a sore tongue, restless legs, or craving ice or non-food items (pica) Mild anaemia may cause no symptoms and only show up on a blood test. Iron deficiency , the most common cause, from: heavy periods (see our guide to period problems ) and pregnancy bleeding from the stomach or bowel , from ulcers, long-term NSAID painkillers, piles, or less often bowel or stomach cancer a diet low in iron, or poor absorption, for example from coeliac disease, H. pylori infection, or long-term acid-reducing medicines hookworm infection, especially in rural communities Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency , from diet, some medicines or pernicious anaemia Thalassaemia , an inherited condition common in Malaysia. Carriers often have small red cells and mild anaemia, with normal iron levels. See our guide to thalassaemia screening . Long-term conditions , including kidney disease and inflammatory diseases A full blood count shows your haemoglobin and the size of your red cells (MCV). See our guide to blood test results . Ferritin is the most useful test for iron stores. Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, but ferritin can look falsely normal during infection or inflammation, so doctors look at the whole picture. Vitamin B12, folate and a thalassaemia test , if needed. Why it matters to find the cause: British gastroenterology guidelines advise that men and women past the menopause with confirmed iron deficiency anaemia should have their stomach and bowel examined by gastroscopy and colonoscopy , as bleeding can be the first sign of cancer. Women who still have periods usually don’t need this unless they have other symptoms. See our guide to bowel cancer . Get tested first. Taking iron without knowing the cause can hide the problem, and iron won’t correct anaemia caused by thalassaemia trait unless you are also low in iron. Dose: usually one tablet once a day. If side effects are a problem, your doctor may suggest every other day or a different preparation. Current guidance has moved away from taking it 2 or 3 times a day. How to take it: ideally on an empty stomach, 30 minutes before food or 2 hours after. Take it with food if it upsets your stomach. Keep it 2 hours apart from tea, coffee, milk, eggs and antacids, which reduce absorption. Side effects: constipation, diarrhoea, nausea and dark stools are common. Tarry black or red stools that may contain blood need a doctor straight away. See our guide to constipation . How long: haemoglobin is usually rechecked within about 4 weeks. Keep taking iron for about 3 months after it returns to normal, to refill your stores. Iron injections or drips are used if tablets aren’t tolerated or don’t work, or if iron is needed quickly. Keep iron tablets locked away from children. An overdose can be fatal for a young child. Diet helps prevent iron deficiency, but tablets are usually needed to treat it. Malaysia’s Recommended Nutrient Intakes list these sources: Haem iron (best absorbed): meat, poultry and fish, including liver, lean beef, ikan bilis , cockles and tenggiri Non-haem iron: leafy greens such as spinach, pucuk paku and kangkung , beans and chickpeas, tofu, eggs, and bread and fortified cereals Eating vitamin C-rich fruit and vegetables, or some meat or fish, with a meal helps absorb non-haem iron. Tea and coffee reduce absorption. In one study, waiting an hour after a meal halved the effect of tea, so have your teh or kopi between meals rather than with them. Avoid liver in pregnancy, as it contains high levels of vitamin A. Vitamin C-rich vegetables and fruit help your body absorb iron from plant foods. Pregnancy: anaemia is linked to heavy bleeding at delivery, low birth weight and premature birth. Malaysian antenatal clinics give iron and folic acid routinely, free at government clinics. Take them as advised, even if they are unpleasant, and tell the clinic if side effects are a problem. See our guide to early pregnancy . Babies and children: a 2022 national survey sample found anaemia in nearly half of children aged 6 to 59 months, although the estimate is uncertain. Anaemia is linked to poorer learning and development. Very large amounts of cow’s milk reduce iron absorption, so offer iron-rich foods. Ask a doctor before giving iron supplements. See a doctor if you feel tired or breathless for no clear reason, have very heavy periods, or look pale. Go to an emergency department if you have black, tarry stools, vomiting blood, heavy bleeding, chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness. See our guide on clinic or emergency department . What is a normal haemoglobin level? At least 13 g/dL in men, 12 g/dL in non-pregnant women and 11 g/dL in pregnancy, according to the World Health Organization. Labs may use slightly different ranges. What are the symptoms of anaemia? Tiredness, shortness of breath, a fast heartbeat, pale skin, headaches and dizziness. What causes iron deficiency? Heavy periods, pregnancy, bleeding from the stomach or bowel, a diet low in iron, or poor absorption. Is kurang darah the same as darah rendah? No. Kurang darah means anaemia. Darah rendah means low blood pressure. How long should I take iron tablets? Usually for about 3 months after your haemoglobin returns to normal, to refill your iron stores. Your doctor will check your progress. How should I take iron tablets? Once a day or on alternate days, ideally on an empty stomach, and 2 hours apart from tea, coffee, milk and antacids. Which foods are high in iron? Meat, liver, fish, ikan bilis and cockles, and plant foods such as spinach, pucuk paku, kangkung, beans and tofu. Should I take iron if I have thalassaemia trait? Only if tests show you are low in iron. Thalassaemia trait causes small red cells, but iron won’t correct it on its own.

title: Pregnancy test and early signs of pregnancy (tanda-tanda hamil): when to test, reading results, and your first antenatal visit
desc: Think you might be pregnant? The early signs, when a home pregnancy test is accurate, what a faint line means, when a blood test is used, what to do after a positive result in Malaysia, including the pink book, and the warning signs that need urgent care.
headings: Early signs of pregnancy (tanda-tanda hamil) · When to take a pregnancy test · Reading the result · Blood pregnancy tests · Positive test? Your next steps in Malaysia · Warning signs in early pregnancy · Unplanned pregnancy and support
keywords: Women's health Pregnancy test and early signs Pregnancy test Tanda-tanda hamil Antenatal care kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp
body: Early signs include a missed period, light spotting, nausea, sore breasts, tiredness and needing to pass urine more often. Many can also happen before a period, so a test is the only way to know. Home pregnancy tests detect the hormone hCG and are about 99% accurate from the first day of a missed period, if used correctly. A faint line usually still means pregnant. A negative result is more likely to be wrong than a positive one, usually because the test was done too early. In Malaysia, register at a Klinik Kesihatan before 12 weeks of pregnancy. You will get the pink book (Buku Pink), free folic acid and iron, and checks for HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis, diabetes and blood pressure. Get emergency care for severe tummy pain on one side, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, dizziness or fainting, which can be signs of an ectopic pregnancy. Symptoms usually start around 4 to 6 weeks after the first day of your last period: a missed period , the most reliable early sign if your cycle is regular very light spotting around the time your period is due (implantation bleeding), which can be mistaken for a light period nausea or vomiting (morning sickness), which can happen at any time of day sore, tender or larger breasts tiredness needing to pass urine more often mood changes, a metallic taste, a stronger sense of smell, cravings, more vaginal discharge or constipation Period or pregnancy? Breast tenderness, tiredness, mood changes and mild cramps can happen before a period too, so symptoms alone can’t tell you whether you are pregnant. Take a test. Pregnancy tests detect hCG , a hormone made once a fertilised egg implants, about 6 days after fertilisation. Levels rise quickly over the following days. Test from the first day of your missed period. If you don’t know when your period is due, test at least 21 days after the last time you had unprotected sex. Some sensitive tests claim to work a few days before a missed period, but they are more likely to give a false negative that early. You can use urine from any time of day. If you are testing early, first-morning urine is the most concentrated. Don’t drink a lot of fluid just before testing. Follow the instructions for how long to wait, and read the result within the time stated, usually within 10 minutes. A faint line that appears much later may be an evaporation line. A faint line within the reading time usually means you are pregnant. hCG may still be low early on. Positive: a positive result is very likely to be right. Rarely, it can follow a very early pregnancy loss (chemical pregnancy) or some fertility treatments that contain hCG. Negative but no period: you may have tested too early. Test again in a few days. If it is still negative and your period hasn’t come, see a doctor. Missed periods without pregnancy can be caused by stress, sudden weight loss or gain, heavy exercise, breastfeeding, hormonal contraception, thyroid problems or PCOS (PMOS) . See a doctor if you have missed 3 periods in a row. See also our guide to thyroid problems . A blood test can detect hCG earlier than a urine test, about 7 to 10 days after conception, and is the only test that measures the exact level. Doctors use it during fertility treatment, if there is bleeding or pain in early pregnancy, or if they suspect a problem such as an ectopic pregnancy. In a healthy early pregnancy, hCG roughly doubles every 2 days, so the test may be repeated to compare. Most women don’t need a blood test to confirm pregnancy. Register for antenatal care before 12 weeks of pregnancy at your nearest Klinik Kesihatan, or with a private doctor. The Ministry of Health counts registration after 12 weeks as late. At your first visit, you will usually have your pregnancy confirmed, your blood pressure, weight and urine checked, an ultrasound, and blood tests including haemoglobin, HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis . You may also be screened for diabetes, depending on your risk. You will be given the pink book (Buku Pink) , your maternal health record. Bring it to every check-up, including at private clinics and hospitals. Government clinics provide folic acid, iron and multivitamins free. Since May 2025, the Tdap vaccine is also offered free in pregnancy. See our guide to the tetanus vaccine . Folic acid: it helps prevent spina bifida and other neural tube defects. The usual dose is 400 micrograms a day , ideally from 3 months before pregnancy until 12 weeks. Women with diabetes, those taking some epilepsy medicines, or who have had a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect need a higher dose prescribed by a doctor. If you didn’t take it before pregnancy, start as soon as you know. Also: stop smoking and vaping, avoid alcohol, and check any medicines with a doctor or pharmacist, but don’t stop prescribed medicines without advice. Use our due date calculator and week-by-week guide to work out how far along you are. Leafy greens contain folate, but a folic acid supplement is still recommended in early pregnancy. Go to an emergency department or call 999 if you have: sudden, severe tummy pain, especially on one side pain in the tip of your shoulder heavy bleeding (soaking a pad soon after putting it on) dizziness or fainting These can be signs of an ectopic pregnancy , where the pregnancy grows outside the womb, usually between 4 and 12 weeks. It can cause dangerous internal bleeding. Get urgent advice for any bleeding or spotting in pregnancy, even without pain. Bleeding isn’t always serious, but it should be checked. Severe vomiting: see a doctor soon if you are vomiting often, can’t keep food or fluids down, or have signs of dehydration such as dark or very little urine and dizziness. This may be hyperemesis gravidarum, which can be treated. If the pregnancy is unplanned or you aren’t sure what to do, you can talk confidentially to a doctor. Other sources of support include: Talian Kasih 15999 (24 hours, or WhatsApp 019-261 5999), the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development’s helpline for counselling and support LPPKN’s KafeTEEN centres, which offer reproductive health services and counselling for young people For preventing pregnancy in future, see our guide to contraception . When can I take a pregnancy test? From the first day of your missed period. If you don’t know when your period is due, wait at least 21 days after unprotected sex. How accurate are home pregnancy tests? About 99% accurate from the first day of a missed period, if used as directed. Negative results are more often wrong than positive ones, usually because the test was done too early. Does a faint line mean I am pregnant? A faint line that appears within the reading time usually means you are pregnant. Lines that appear long after may be evaporation lines. What are the early signs of pregnancy? A missed period, light spotting, nausea, sore breasts, tiredness and needing to pass urine more often, usually from about 4 to 6 weeks. Can I tell if I am pregnant before my period is due? Not reliably. Early symptoms are similar to those before a period, and tests are less accurate before a missed period. When should I go to the clinic after a positive test? Register for antenatal care before 12 weeks of pregnancy at a Klinik Kesihatan or private clinic. Go to an emergency department straight away for severe pain, heavy bleeding or fainting. How much folic acid should I take? Usually 400 micrograms a day from before pregnancy until 12 weeks. Some women, such as those with diabetes or a previous neural tube defect pregnancy, need a higher dose from a doctor. What is the pink book? Buku Pink is your maternal health record in Malaysia, given when you register your pregnancy. Bring it to every antenatal check-up.

title: Semut charlie (Paederus) rash: what it looks like, first aid, treatment and keeping the beetles away
desc: Woke up with a burning red streak or blisters on your neck or arm? It may be semut charlie. The insect doesn’t bite: the rash comes from a toxin released when it is crushed on the skin. What to do straight away, how the rash is treated, why the eyes are at risk, and how to keep the beetles out.
headings: What is semut charlie? · What the rash looks like · First aid · Treatment · Keeping semut charlie away
keywords: Aesthetics & skin Semut charlie rash Paederus dermatitis Semut charlie Rove beetle aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Semut charlie is a rove beetle (Paederus), about 7 to 10 mm long, with an orange body, black head and dark blue wing cases. It is attracted to bright lights at night. It doesn’t bite. The rash comes from a toxin in its body fluid when it is crushed or rubbed on the skin. The rash usually appears within 1 to 2 days: a burning red streak or patch, often on the neck, face or arms, which then blisters. If one lands on you, blow or flick it off rather than crushing it. If it was crushed, wash the skin straight away with soap and water. Keep it away from your eyes, which can become badly inflamed. See a doctor for any eye symptoms or widespread blisters. Semut charlie is a rove beetle , Paederus fuscipes , not an ant. It is about 7 to 10 mm long, with a black head, an orange body, shiny dark blue wing cases and a black tip. When disturbed it may raise its tail, like a scorpion. It lives in rice fields and other vegetation, where it actually helps by eating crop pests. It flies into homes, especially during heavy rain, floods and the rice harvest, and is strongly attracted to bright lights at night. A Universiti Sains Malaysia study in Penang found far more beetles around bright lights than dim ones, and more on higher floors. It doesn’t bite or sting . Its body fluid contains pederin , a toxin made by bacteria living inside female beetles. The toxin is released when the beetle is crushed or rubbed against the skin. Outbreaks in Malaysia have included about 2,000 people in high-rise flats and school hostels in Penang in 2002, 360 cases in university hostels next to an oil palm estate in Selangor in 2010, and 21 cases in Kelantan in mid-2019, mostly in schools. It usually appears within 1 to 2 days of contact, often noticed on waking. It starts as a burning, stinging red streak or patch , often in a line where the beetle was smeared across the skin (sometimes called a “whiplash” mark). Blisters and small pus spots form over the next few days, then dry and crust. “Kissing” lesions appear where two skin surfaces touch, such as inside the elbow or between the thighs, because the toxin transfers between them. It most often affects the face, neck, shoulders and arms. The toxin can be spread to other parts of the body on your fingers, including the genitals. The rash is often mistaken for shingles, burns or other rashes. See our guides to shingles (kayap) and itchy skin . The eyes: rubbing your eyes with contaminated fingers can cause painful swelling of the eyelids and inflammation of the eye (sometimes called “Nairobi eye”), which can temporarily affect vision. Don’t crush or slap the beetle. Blow it away or flick it off, or pick it up with a tissue. If it was crushed or crawled on your skin, wash the area straight away with soap and plenty of water . Wash your hands and keep them away from your eyes. If any got near your eyes, rinse them gently with clean water. Wash any clothes or bedding the beetle was crushed on separately. Cool, wet compresses soothe the burning. A doctor will usually prescribe a steroid cream to calm the inflammation, and an antihistamine tablet for itch. See our guide to antihistamines . Antibiotics are only needed if the blisters become infected, with spreading redness, pus or fever. Don’t scratch, and don’t burst the blisters. Home remedies such as toothpaste don’t help and can irritate the skin further. Most rashes heal within 1 to 3 weeks . Dark marks can last for several months, especially on darker skin, and fade slowly. See a doctor if: your eye or eyelid is red, swollen or painful, or your vision is affected the rash is large, very painful or blistering widely, or on the face or genitals it looks infected a child is affected A GP can confirm the rash and prescribe a steroid cream, which helps it settle faster. Switch off lights you aren’t using at night, especially near open windows, and sleep with the lights off. Close windows and doors at night, or fit fine insect screens. Use warm-coloured or LED lights rather than bright white fluorescent tubes, which attract more beetles. Use a bed net in hostels and homes where beetles are common. Shake out bedding, towels and clothes before using them. Cut back vegetation close to buildings. In outbreaks, local councils and health offices may carry out insecticide spraying. Semut charlie rash isn’t spread from person to person, and it has nothing to do with hygiene. Anyone in an area with the beetles can be affected. Does semut charlie bite? No. It doesn’t bite or sting. The rash is caused by a toxin in its body fluid, released when the beetle is crushed or rubbed on the skin. What does a semut charlie rash look like? A burning red streak or patch, often in a line, that appears within 1 to 2 days and then blisters. It is common on the neck, face and arms. What should I do if semut charlie lands on me? Blow or flick it off without crushing it. If it was crushed, wash the skin straight away with soap and water, and wash your hands. How long does a semut charlie rash take to heal? Usually 1 to 3 weeks. Dark marks may take several months to fade. Is semut charlie dangerous for the eyes? Yes. Rubbing the toxin into the eyes can cause painful eyelid swelling and eye inflammation. See a doctor promptly. What cream is used for semut charlie rash? A doctor usually prescribes a steroid cream, sometimes with an antihistamine for itch, and antibiotics only if the blisters get infected. Why are there so many semut charlie at night? They are attracted to bright lights, especially during the rainy season and rice harvest, and fly into homes near fields and vegetation. Is semut charlie rash contagious? No. It comes only from contact with the beetle’s toxin and doesn’t spread from person to person.

title: Skin tags, keloids, lipomas and moles (tahi lalat): what they are, removal options, and which lumps need checking
desc: Most skin lumps and bumps are harmless, but some need checking. What skin tags, keloids, lipomas and moles are, how doctors remove them, why you shouldn’t cut them off yourself or have them removed at a beauty salon, and the warning signs of skin cancer.
headings: Skin tags · Keloids (parut keloid) · Lipomas · Moles (tahi lalat) and the warning signs of melanoma · Mole removal: safely, by a doctor
keywords: Aesthetics & skin Skin tags, keloids, lipomas and moles Skin tag Keloid Lipoma kencing manis gula hba1c payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Skin tags are small, soft flaps of skin in folds such as the neck and armpits. They are harmless, and are linked to weight, type 2 diabetes and pregnancy. Keloids are raised scars that grow beyond the original wound. They are more common in Asian skin, and often come back after removal, so treatment usually combines steroid injections and other methods. Lipomas are soft, movable fatty lumps. See a doctor for any lump that is larger than about 5 cm, hard, fixed, painful or growing. Check moles using ABCDE: asymmetry, irregular border, several colours, diameter over 6 mm, and evolving (changing). In Asians, melanoma often appears on the soles, palms or under the nails. In Malaysia, aesthetic procedures must be done by registered, credentialed doctors at licensed clinics, not at beauty salons. Suspicious moles should be cut out and sent to a lab, not lasered. Skin tags are small, soft, skin-coloured or slightly darker growths, from 2 mm to a few centimetres, that hang from the skin on a thin stalk. They form where skin rubs: the neck, armpits, eyelids, under the breasts, groin and around the bottom. They are more common with excess weight, type 2 diabetes or insulin resistance, and in pregnancy. Lots of skin tags can be a reason to check your blood sugar: see our guide to normal blood sugar levels . They are harmless and don’t need removing, but they can catch on clothing or jewellery. Removal: a doctor can snip them off, freeze them or remove them with heat (cautery), usually in minutes under local anaesthetic. They don’t usually come back, though new ones may form. Removal can leave a small scar or a darker mark, especially on brown skin. Don’t cut or tie off skin tags yourself , as they can bleed and become infected. Other growths, such as warts and seborrhoeic keratoses, can look similar. See our guide to warts . A soft lump around the anus may be a skin tag left after piles: see our guide to piles (buasir) . A keloid is a raised, firm, often shiny scar that keeps growing beyond the edges of the original wound. A hypertrophic scar looks similar but stays within the wound and often flattens with time. Keloids are more common in darker and Asian skin , usually appear between puberty and 30, and can run in families. DermNet notes they are more common in people of Chinese origin than in those of Malay or Indian origin. Common sites are the chest, shoulders, upper back, neck and earlobes . They can follow ear piercings, acne, chickenpox, burns, vaccinations or surgery. See our guide to acne . They can be itchy or tender, but aren’t dangerous. Treatment aims to flatten and soften the scar. No single treatment works best: Steroid injections into the keloid are the most common, often every 4 to 6 weeks for several months. Up to half come back afterwards. Silicone gel or sheets and pressure dressings, used daily for months. Freezing , laser or other injections. Surgery alone often makes the keloid come back bigger , so it is combined with injections or radiotherapy afterwards. If you are prone to keloids , avoid tattoos, piercings and cosmetic procedures you don’t need, treat acne early, and tell any doctor before surgery. A lipoma is a soft, rubbery, slow-growing lump of fat under the skin that moves slightly when pressed. They are common on the shoulders, back, chest, arms and thighs, and are usually painless and harmless. They are more common in people with high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes or obesity. Removal is optional. A doctor can cut it out under local anaesthetic, and it may be sent to a lab to confirm what it is. Liposuction is an option for some, but they come back more often. See a doctor promptly for a lump that: is larger than about 5 cm (a golf ball) is growing is hard , fixed, or deep under the muscle is painful, red or hot has come back after removal These can occasionally be signs of a rare cancer called a soft tissue sarcoma, and need a scan. Other common lumps include skin cysts , which shouldn’t be squeezed, and boils . Most moles are harmless. They are often darker on brown skin, new ones appear in childhood and the teens, and they can darken slightly in pregnancy. Use ABCDE to check your moles: Sign What to look for A symmetry The two halves look different B order Ragged, notched or blurred edges C olour Two or more colours, or uneven shading D iameter Larger than about 6 mm (a pencil eraser) E volving Changing in size, shape or colour Also see a doctor for a mole that looks different from your others, or that itches, bleeds, crusts or becomes sore. In Asian skin, look at your feet, hands and nails. Melanoma on the soles, palms and under the nails (acral melanoma) makes up a larger share of melanomas in Asian people. At Sarawak General Hospital, 62% of melanomas from 2003 to 2009 were acral, mostly on the heel and sole, and most were found at an advanced stage. Check for: a new or changing dark patch on the sole or palm a dark streak in a nail that is wider than 3 mm, uneven or growing, or where the dark colour spreads onto the skin around the nail, not caused by an injury Other skin cancers, basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, often appear as a pearly or scaly lump or a sore that doesn’t heal, usually on the face. In a recent Sarawak study, these were more common than melanoma. A doctor can examine a mole with a dermatoscope and decide whether it needs removing and testing. Suspicious moles are cut out whole and sent to a laboratory to check for cancer. Lasering or burning away a mole destroys it without testing, which could miss a melanoma. Harmless raised moles can be shaved off for cosmetic reasons, which may leave a small mark. Avoid creams or online products that claim to remove moles or skin tags. They can burn the skin and scar, and they leave nothing to test. Choose a registered doctor, not a beauty salon. Under Malaysian Medical Council and Ministry of Health guidelines, aesthetic medical procedures must be carried out by registered doctors who hold a Letter of Credentialing and Privileging (LCP) for the procedure, at licensed clinics. The Ministry of Health has warned against aesthetic treatments, including lasers, at beauty salons, spas and other unregistered premises, which risk complications and disability. Ask to see the doctor’s practising certificate and credentials. What causes skin tags? Friction where skin rubs together. They are more common with excess weight, type 2 diabetes and in pregnancy, and are harmless. Can I remove a skin tag myself? It isn’t recommended, as it can bleed and get infected. A doctor can remove it quickly by snipping, freezing or cautery. Why do keloids keep coming back? Keloids grow from an overactive healing response. Surgery alone often triggers a bigger keloid, so it is combined with steroid injections or other treatments, and up to half come back. Is a lipoma dangerous? Lipomas are almost always harmless. See a doctor for a lump that is larger than about 5 cm, hard, fixed, painful or growing. How do I know if a mole is cancerous? Use ABCDE: asymmetry, irregular border, several colours, diameter over 6 mm, and evolving. See a doctor for any mole that changes, itches or bleeds. Can melanoma appear on the feet? Yes. In Asian people, melanoma is relatively often found on the soles, palms or under the nails, and is often diagnosed late. Can I have a mole removed at a beauty salon? No. In Malaysia, aesthetic procedures must be done by credentialed doctors at licensed clinics. Suspicious moles should be removed and sent for testing. Should moles be removed by laser? Not if there is any doubt about them. Suspicious moles should be cut out and tested in a lab, which laser removal doesn’t allow.

title: GERD and acid reflux (pedih ulu hati): symptoms, triggers, medicines and when it’s more serious
desc: Burning in the chest after meals, a sour taste or a cough that won’t go away can all be acid reflux. What GERD is, the lifestyle changes with the best evidence, how to use antacids and acid-reducing medicines properly, H. pylori, and the warning signs that need a scope or emergency care.
headings: What is GERD? · Heartburn or heart attack? · Lifestyle changes that help · Medicines for reflux (ubat gastrik) · When you need a scope (endoscopy) · H. pylori · Reflux in pregnancy
keywords: Guides GERD and acid reflux Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Heartburn Helicobacter pylori kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital
body: Typical GERD symptoms are a burning feeling in the middle of the chest (heartburn) and acid or food coming back up, often after meals or when lying down. Some people have a cough, hoarse voice or sore throat instead. Chest pain that feels tight or heavy, or spreads to the arm, neck or jaw, could be a heart attack. Call 999. Losing weight if overweight, not eating 3 hours before bed, raising the head of the bed and stopping smoking all help. Antacids give quick relief. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, are the main treatment for frequent symptoms. See a doctor for difficulty swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools, anaemia, or new symptoms after middle age, which may need an endoscopy. A ring of muscle at the bottom of the food pipe normally stops stomach contents flowing back up. In GERD , acid escapes upwards often enough to cause troublesome symptoms or damage. Occasional heartburn after a big meal is common and isn’t GERD. Symptoms: heartburn ( pedih ulu hati ): a burning feeling in the middle of the chest acid or food coming back up into the throat or mouth (regurgitation), and a sour or bitter taste symptoms that are worse after eating, when lying down or bending over a long-lasting cough, hoarse voice, sore throat, hiccups or bad breath bloating and nausea GERD vs “gastric”: in Malaysia, “gastric” is often used for any upper tummy discomfort. Doctors call this dyspepsia , which can come from reflux, stomach ulcers, H. pylori infection, medicines, or occasionally something more serious. See our guide to stomach pain and “gastric” . In Southeast Asia , a 2021 regional consensus found GERD is becoming more common, but is mostly mild, without visible damage to the food pipe. A heart attack can feel like indigestion or a burning in the chest. Call 999 if chest pain: feels tight, heavy or squeezing spreads to the arm, neck, jaw, back or stomach comes with breathlessness, sweating, nausea or feeling faint doesn’t settle quickly, or comes on with exertion Don’t assume it is “gastric”, especially if you have diabetes, high blood pressure, smoke or are older. See our guide to the warning signs of a heart attack . Lose weight if you are overweight. This has the strongest evidence. More than half of Malaysian adults are overweight or obese: see our BMI calculator . Don’t eat for 3 hours before bed , and have smaller meals rather than big ones, especially late at night (including supper). Raise the head of your bed by 10 to 20 cm with blocks under the legs, rather than piling up pillows, if symptoms are worse at night. Sleeping on your left side may reduce night-time reflux, though the evidence is limited. Stop smoking and cut down on alcohol. Notice your own triggers. Common ones include coffee, alcohol, chocolate, tomatoes, fatty and spicy food, but you don’t need to cut out foods that don’t bother you. Avoid tight belts and waistbands. Losing weight is the lifestyle change with the strongest evidence for reducing reflux. Medicine How it helps Notes Antacids and alginates (liquids, chewable tablets) Neutralise acid or form a protective layer on top of the stomach contents. Work within minutes Take after meals or when symptoms start. For occasional use. Some contain a lot of sodium, so check with a pharmacist if you have heart or kidney problems H2 blockers (such as famotidine) Reduce acid production An alternative for milder or night-time symptoms Proton pump inhibitors, PPIs (such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole) Strongly reduce acid production The main treatment for frequent symptoms. Usually a 4 to 8 week course Taking PPIs properly: Take them 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast (or before your evening meal if advised). They work best on an empty stomach before food. They take a few days to work fully. After a course, your doctor may try stepping down to the lowest dose that works, or stopping. When you stop, acid symptoms can briefly return (rebound) for a week or two, which doesn’t mean you still need them. Long-term PPIs are safe for most people who need them. Some studies have linked long-term use to low vitamin B12 and weaker bones, but don’t stop them on your own if a doctor has prescribed them for a reason. Review them with your doctor at least yearly. Don’t use pharmacy PPIs for more than 2 weeks without seeing a doctor. See a doctor soon if you have reflux or “gastric” symptoms with: difficulty or pain when swallowing, or food sticking weight loss without trying vomiting blood or what looks like coffee grounds, or black, tarry stools (go to an emergency department) anaemia, or feeling very tired and breathless persistent vomiting new symptoms starting in middle age , or a family history of stomach cancer symptoms that don’t improve with treatment The doctor may refer you for an endoscopy (a thin camera passed through the mouth into the stomach). Stomach cancer is more common in Asia than in the West and can occur at a younger age, so Asian experts suggest a lower age threshold for checking new symptoms. Barrett’s oesophagus, a change in the lining of the food pipe caused by long-term reflux, is rare in Southeast Asia. Helicobacter pylori is a bacterium that infects the stomach lining. It causes most stomach ulcers and is a major risk factor for stomach cancer. Clearing it largely stops ulcers from coming back. In Malaysia , studies have found infection rates of about 10 to 25% in Malays, 35 to 55% in Chinese, 50 to 60% in Indians, and higher in some indigenous communities in Sabah and Sarawak. Rates have fallen over time. It is tested with a breath test or stool test , or a biopsy during endoscopy. Stop PPIs for at least 2 weeks and antibiotics for 4 weeks before a breath or stool test, or the result may be falsely negative. Ask your doctor before stopping. Treatment is a 1 to 2 week course of two antibiotics plus a PPI, followed by a test to confirm it has gone. Heartburn is common in pregnancy because of hormones and the growing baby pressing on the stomach. Eat small meals, avoid eating within 3 hours of bed, and raise your head and shoulders at night. Antacids or alginates are often suitable, but check with a pharmacist or doctor first, and take them at least 2 hours apart from iron or folic acid tablets. See our pregnancy week-by-week guide . What is GERD? Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: stomach acid flowing back into the food pipe often enough to cause heartburn, regurgitation or other symptoms. What does pedih ulu hati mean? It is heartburn: a burning feeling in the middle of the chest or upper tummy, often caused by acid reflux. How can I tell heartburn from a heart attack? You can’t always tell. Chest pain that is tight or heavy, spreads to the arm, neck or jaw, or comes with breathlessness or sweating needs a 999 call. What is the best medicine for GERD? Antacids give quick relief for occasional symptoms. For frequent symptoms, a PPI taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal for 4 to 8 weeks is the main treatment. Can GERD be cured? Many people control it well with weight loss, meal timing and medicine, and some can stop medicine after a course. It can come back. Is it safe to take PPIs long term? For most people who need them, yes. Have your doctor review them regularly and use the lowest dose that works. How is H. pylori tested? With a breath test, stool test or biopsy during endoscopy. Stop PPIs for 2 weeks before a breath or stool test, after checking with your doctor. When does gastric pain need a scope? With difficulty swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools, anaemia, new symptoms in middle age, a family history of stomach cancer, or symptoms that don’t improve.

title: Allergies and resdung (allergic rhinitis): antihistamines explained, nasal sprays and sinusitis
desc: Constant sneezing, a runny or blocked nose and itchy eyes are often allergies, and in Malaysia the main culprit is house dust mites. What resdung is, how the common antihistamines compare, why a steroid nasal spray often works better, the decongestant trap, and how to tell sinusitis from allergies.
headings: What is resdung (allergic rhinitis)? · Antihistamines compared: cetirizine, loratadine and chlorpheniramine · Nasal sprays and rinses · Reducing dust mites and other triggers · Sinusitis or allergies? · Severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis)
keywords: Guides Allergies, resdung and antihistamines Allergic rhinitis Resdung Antihistamines jerebu api ipu air pollutant index smoke darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Allergic rhinitis causes sneezing, an itchy, runny or blocked nose and itchy, watery eyes. In Malaysia, house dust mites are the most common trigger, followed by cockroaches and pet fur. Non-drowsy antihistamines such as cetirizine and loratadine work about equally well. Cetirizine is a little more likely to cause sleepiness. Chlorpheniramine is an older antihistamine that causes drowsiness, so it isn’t recommended for allergic rhinitis by Malaysian allergy specialists. Don’t drive after taking it. A steroid nasal spray works better than antihistamine tablets for a blocked nose and persistent symptoms, but takes 1 to 2 weeks of regular use for full effect. Decongestant nasal sprays should be used for no more than 5 to 7 days, or they can make the blockage worse. In allergic rhinitis, the immune system overreacts to harmless particles in the air, called allergens, causing inflammation in the nose. Symptoms start within minutes of contact: sneezing, often in bouts an itchy, runny or blocked nose itchy, red, watery eyes. See our guide to red eyes . an itchy throat or roof of the mouth, and a cough from mucus dripping down the throat tiredness and poor sleep, which can affect work and school In Malaysia , symptoms often last all year rather than coming in seasons. The Malaysian Society of Allergy and Immunology says the humid climate favours house dust mites , and cockroaches and animal fur are also major allergens. In a study of children with rhinitis at Hospital UKM, about 7 in 10 were allergic to house dust mites. Allergic rhinitis often goes with asthma and eczema , and can make asthma harder to control. See our guide to eczema and hives . Haze and smoke can irritate the nose and make symptoms worse: see our haze guide . Antihistamines block histamine, a chemical released during an allergic reaction. They help sneezing, itching, a runny nose and itchy eyes, and also hives , but they don’t do much for a blocked nose. Cetirizine Loratadine Chlorpheniramine Type Non-drowsy (second generation) Non-drowsy (second generation) Drowsy (first generation) Usual adult dose 10 mg once a day 10 mg once a day 4 mg every 4 to 6 hours, no more than 24 mg a day Drowsiness Can cause sleepiness in some people, more than loratadine Least likely to cause sleepiness Often causes drowsiness. Don’t drive or operate machinery Notes Works within about an hour Similar effect to cetirizine Not recommended for allergic rhinitis by Malaysian allergy specialists Other non-drowsy antihistamines include fexofenadine, desloratadine and levocetirizine . According to the NHS, they all seem to work about as well as each other, so the choice depends on side effects and what suits you. Avoid alcohol with antihistamines, as it increases drowsiness. Children: doses depend on age and weight, and young children usually need a liquid. Malaysia’s Drug Control Authority says cough and cold medicines containing antihistamines shouldn’t be given to children under 2, and only on a doctor’s or pharmacist’s advice for those aged 2 to 6. Ask a pharmacist for the right product and dose. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: the NHS considers cetirizine and loratadine reasonable choices, but some manufacturers advise avoiding them, so check with your doctor or pharmacist first. In Malaysia, these antihistamines are supplied by pharmacists, without a doctor’s prescription. Steroid nasal sprays are the most effective treatment for persistent or moderate to severe allergic rhinitis, and work better than antihistamine tablets for a blocked nose. The Malaysian allergy consensus recommends them as a main treatment. They start working within hours, but give their full effect after 1 to 2 weeks of daily use , so keep using them. Side effects are mostly local, such as dryness and the occasional nosebleed. How to use: blow your nose, tilt your head slightly forward, close one nostril, put the nozzle in the other nostril pointing slightly outwards (away from the middle of the nose), spray while breathing in gently, then breathe out through your mouth. See a doctor if there is no improvement after 1 to 2 weeks. Decongestant nasal sprays (such as xylometazoline) clear a blocked nose quickly, but don’t use them for more than 5 to 7 days . Longer use can cause rebound congestion that makes the blockage worse. They aren’t suitable for young children. Oral decongestant tablets aren’t suitable for young children or in pregnancy, and people with high blood pressure should ask a pharmacist first. Salt-water (saline) rinses or sprays wash out allergens and mucus and are safe to use regularly. Use allergy-proof covers on mattresses and pillows. Wash bedding weekly in hot water (60°C or above) . Dust with a damp cloth and vacuum regularly, ideally with a HEPA filter. Reduce soft toys, carpets and clutter in the bedroom. Keep the home dry and well ventilated, and deal with damp and mould. Keep pets out of the bedroom, and control cockroaches. Allergy testing (a skin prick test or blood test) can identify your triggers. For severe allergic rhinitis that doesn’t improve with a steroid spray and antihistamines, specialists may offer allergen immunotherapy , injections or tablets under the tongue that gradually reduce the allergy over several years. Haze doesn’t cause allergies, but it can irritate the nose and make allergic rhinitis worse. Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, usually after a cold. It causes a blocked nose, thick yellow or green mucus, pain or pressure around the cheeks, eyes or forehead, a reduced sense of smell, and sometimes fever. Most sinusitis is caused by viruses and clears within 2 to 4 weeks without antibiotics . Only a small minority of cases are bacterial. Saline rinses, painkillers and a steroid nasal spray can help. Antibiotics are considered for severe symptoms, or symptoms lasting more than about 10 days and getting worse. See a doctor if symptoms last more than 3 weeks or keep coming back. Sinusitis lasting more than 3 months may need an ENT specialist. Get urgent help for swelling or redness around the eye, double or reduced vision, a severe headache, a stiff neck, confusion or a very high fever. A cold usually clears in about a week. Allergies tend to cause more sneezing and itching, clear runny mucus, no fever, and last as long as you are exposed to the trigger. See also our guides to flu and a cough that won’t go away . Call 999 immediately for swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or wheezing, difficulty swallowing, feeling faint, or pale or blue lips, especially after a food, medicine or insect sting. If the person has an adrenaline auto-injector, use it straight away, then lie them down with their legs raised. Antihistamine tablets are not enough for anaphylaxis. What is resdung in English? Resdung usually refers to allergic rhinitis: sneezing, an itchy, runny or blocked nose caused by an allergy, often to house dust mites. What is cetirizine used for? It is a non-drowsy antihistamine for allergic rhinitis, hives and itchy skin. The usual adult dose is 10 mg once a day. Cetirizine or loratadine: which is better? They work about equally well. Cetirizine is slightly more likely to cause sleepiness, so loratadine may suit people who need to stay alert. Does chlorpheniramine make you sleepy? Yes, it is an older antihistamine that often causes drowsiness. Don’t drive or operate machinery after taking it. What is the best treatment for a blocked nose from allergies? A steroid nasal spray used every day. It takes 1 to 2 weeks to work fully. Antihistamine tablets help less with blockage. How long can I use a decongestant nasal spray? No more than 5 to 7 days. Longer use can cause rebound congestion that makes your nose more blocked. Do I need antibiotics for sinusitis? Usually not. Most sinusitis is viral and clears within 2 to 4 weeks. Antibiotics are considered for severe or worsening symptoms after about 10 days. Can I take antihistamines while pregnant? Some, such as loratadine and cetirizine, are often considered suitable, but check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

title: Slipped disc and sciatica (sakit pinggang): symptoms, what helps, and red flags
desc: Back pain that shoots down your leg is often sciatica from a slipped disc. Most people recover within weeks to a few months without surgery. What a slipped disc is, what actually helps, when scans and surgery are needed, the emergency signs not to ignore, and why to avoid unlicensed bone-setting.
headings: What is a slipped disc? · Symptoms of a slipped disc and sciatica · Red flags: when to go to hospital · What helps · Physiotherapy, injections and surgery · Preventing back problems
keywords: Guides Slipped disc and sciatica Herniated disc Sciatica Low back pain kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp
body: A slipped (herniated or prolapsed) disc doesn’t actually slip: its soft centre bulges through the tough outer layer. Many people have disc bulges on a scan without any pain. Sciatica is pain, tingling or numbness down the back of one leg, often worse than the back pain, and worse with coughing or sneezing. Most people improve within a few weeks to a few months. Keep moving: bed rest doesn’t help. Scans usually aren’t needed at first. Physiotherapy and exercise are the main treatments, with injections or surgery for severe pain that doesn’t improve. Go to an emergency department for numbness around the bottom or genitals, problems passing urine or controlling the bladder or bowels, or weakness in both legs. Between each bone of the spine is a disc, a cushion with a tough outer ring and a soft, jelly-like centre. In a slipped disc (also called a herniated or prolapsed disc), the centre bulges or pushes through the outer ring. It most often happens in the lower back, at the two lowest levels, and less often in the neck. It only causes symptoms if it presses on or irritates a nerve. Disc bulges are very common with age: in one large review of scans, they were seen in 30% of 20-year-olds and 84% of 80-year-olds with no back pain at all . So a bulge on a scan doesn’t always explain pain. Low back pain is very common in Malaysia. A 2023 review of Malaysian studies found high rates among nurses and drivers in particular, linked to age, weight, heavy lifting, posture and long working hours. lower back pain, sometimes sudden after lifting or bending sciatica : pain in the buttock and down the back of one leg, sometimes into the foot. It can be sharp, shooting or burning, and the leg pain is often worse than the back pain. tingling, pins and needles or numbness in the leg or foot weakness in the leg or foot pain that is worse when coughing, sneezing or sitting for a long time A slipped disc in the neck causes neck pain with pain, tingling or weakness down the arm and into the hand. Go to an emergency department straight away (don’t drive yourself) if you have back pain with: numbness or tingling around your bottom, genitals or inner thighs (saddle numbness) difficulty passing urine, or loss of control of your bladder or bowels sciatica in both legs , or severe or worsening weakness in your legs or feet back pain after a serious fall or accident These can be signs of cauda equina syndrome , where the nerves at the bottom of the spine are badly squashed. It needs emergency surgery to prevent permanent damage. See a doctor soon for back pain with fever, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, a swelling in the back, or pain that is worse at night or doesn’t ease with rest. See our guide on clinic or emergency department . Stay active. Keep moving and carry on with daily activities as much as you can. Bed rest doesn’t speed recovery and can slow it. Avoid sitting or lying still for long . Get up and walk regularly. Heat , such as a heat pack or warm shower, can ease muscle spasm. Gentle exercise and stretches , and return to work as soon as you can, with adjustments if needed. Painkillers: the UK’s NICE guideline advises against paracetamol on its own for low back pain, as it doesn’t help much. Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) can help back pain at the lowest dose for the shortest time, though the benefit for sciatica is limited. Avoid long-term strong opioid painkillers. NICE also advises against nerve-pain medicines such as gabapentin and pregabalin for sciatica, as there is no overall evidence of benefit and some evidence of harm. Discuss options with your doctor. Staying active and exercising helps recovery more than bed rest. Scans: an MRI usually isn’t needed in the first weeks unless there are red flags. It is used if symptoms don’t improve, or if an injection or surgery is being considered. Physiotherapy and exercise are the main treatment. Hands-on therapy such as manipulation or massage may help as part of an exercise programme, not on its own. Back belts and corsets aren’t recommended. Epidural steroid injection: an injection near the nerve may be considered for severe, acute sciatica. Surgery (usually a microdiscectomy, removing the part of the disc pressing on the nerve) is considered when severe leg pain doesn’t improve with other treatment, or urgently for red flags. In a major trial, early surgery relieved leg pain faster, but after a year outcomes were similar to waiting, and most people in both groups had recovered. In Malaysia , care usually starts with a GP, who can refer you to physiotherapy at a government health clinic or hospital, or to an orthopaedic or spine specialist. Be cautious with unlicensed bone-setting or forceful manipulation for a suspected slipped disc. A Malaysian orthopaedic surgeon has warned that patients have been made worse, with a risk of nerve damage. See a doctor first. Lift with your legs: bend your knees, keep the load close to your body, and avoid twisting. Take regular breaks from sitting and driving, and use back support when seated. Stay active and keep to a healthy weight. See our BMI calculator . Stop smoking, which is linked to disc problems. Workers injured at work may be covered by PERKESO, which runs rehabilitation and return-to-work services. What is a slipped disc? A bulge of the soft centre of a spinal disc through its outer layer, which can press on a nerve. It is also called a herniated or prolapsed disc. What are the signs of a slipped disc? Back pain with pain, tingling or numbness running down one leg (sciatica), often worse when coughing, sneezing or sitting. How long does a slipped disc take to heal? Most people improve within a few weeks to a few months without surgery. Should I rest in bed with a slipped disc? No. Staying as active as you can helps more than bed rest. Avoid sitting or lying still for long periods. Do I need an MRI for sciatica? Usually not at first. An MRI is used if there are red flags, if symptoms don’t improve, or before an injection or surgery. When does a slipped disc need surgery? When severe leg pain or weakness doesn’t improve with other treatment, or urgently for red flags such as bladder or bowel problems. When is back pain an emergency? With numbness around the bottom or genitals, problems passing urine or controlling the bladder or bowels, weakness in both legs, or after a serious accident. Is massage or bone-setting good for a slipped disc? Unlicensed bone-setting or forceful manipulation can make things worse. Hands-on therapy may help as part of an exercise programme from a qualified physiotherapist.

title: G6PD deficiency in Malaysia: newborn screening, jaundice, what to avoid, and living with it
desc: About 3 in 100 Malaysian babies are born with G6PD deficiency. What it means, why newborns are watched closely for jaundice, which medicines and substances really need avoiding (mothballs and fava beans top the list), which food lists are myths, and the warning signs of a crisis.
headings: What is G6PD deficiency? (G6PD maksud) · Newborn screening in Malaysia · G6PD deficiency and jaundice in babies · What to avoid · Signs of a haemolytic crisis · Living with G6PD deficiency
keywords: Prevention G6PD deficiency G6PD deficiency Neonatal jaundice Haemolysis payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: G6PD deficiency affects about 3 in 100 Malaysian newborns. It is more common in boys, and in Chinese and Malay than Indian families, but girls can be affected too. All babies in Malaysia are screened using blood from the umbilical cord at birth. The result is recorded in the child’s health record book. Babies with G6PD deficiency are more likely to develop severe jaundice, so they are monitored closely in the first days of life. The best-proven triggers are fava beans (broad beans), naphthalene mothballs, henna, infections and a short list of medicines. Many food “avoid lists” circulating online have little evidence. Tell every doctor and pharmacist that you or your child has G6PD deficiency before taking any new medicine or supplement. G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) is an enzyme that protects red blood cells from damage. People with G6PD deficiency have too little of it, so when they are exposed to certain triggers, their red cells can break down quickly. This is called haemolysis , and it causes anaemia and jaundice. It is inherited through a gene on the X chromosome, so it is more common and usually more severe in boys. Girls who carry the gene can also be affected, sometimes as much as boys. Worldwide, at least 400 million people have it. In Malaysia, studies put it at about 3 to 4% of newborns, more common in Chinese and Malay than Indian families. It is lifelong, but it isn’t a disease you “catch”, and most people with it live completely normal, healthy lives. Malaysia has screened newborns for G6PD deficiency since 1986. Under the Ministry of Health programme, blood is taken from the umbilical cord right after birth and tested for G6PD deficiency, together with congenital hypothyroidism. The result is recorded in your child’s health record book ( Buku Rekod Kesihatan Kanak-kanak ). Keep it safe and show it to doctors. The standard screening test can miss partial deficiency , which is more common in girls. If a girl has unexplained jaundice or anaemia, or there is a family history, ask the doctor whether more testing is needed. Babies with G6PD deficiency are more likely to develop severe newborn jaundice . Untreated, very high levels of bilirubin (the yellow pigment) can cause brain damage (kernicterus) and hearing loss. That is why these babies are watched closely and have their bilirubin checked in the first days of life, and may stay in hospital a little longer. Jaundice is treated with light therapy (phototherapy). See a doctor urgently if your baby: has yellow skin or eyes that are spreading or getting deeper is very sleepy, floppy or feeding poorly looks pale, has dark urine, or has any breathing difficulty or fits For babies with G6PD deficiency: Don’t store the baby’s clothes, or yours, with mothballs (naphthalene, ubat gegat) , and don’t use them in the home. Avoid henna on the baby or on a breastfeeding mother. Check with a doctor before giving the baby, or taking while breastfeeding, any herbal or traditional medicine. Some Chinese herbal medicines, such as those containing huang lian (Coptis), have been linked to severe jaundice in babies with G6PD deficiency. Breastfeeding mothers are generally advised to avoid the same triggers as the baby. See also our guide to fever in children , as infections can also trigger haemolysis. A 2016 systematic review by a Malaysian-led team found that the triggers with consistent evidence are: Fava beans (broad beans, sometimes called kacang parang ), including foods made from fava bean flour or protein. Cooking doesn’t make them safe. Check labels. Naphthalene mothballs Henna certain chemical dyes Infections are also a common trigger, so see a doctor if a person with G6PD deficiency is unwell with a fever. Medicines: an international pharmacogenetics guideline (CPIC) lists a small number of medicines as high risk, including dapsone, primaquine, tafenoquine, rasburicase and methylene blue , with nitrofurantoin to be used with caution.
